a: In the third year of Hoshea
t: Hezekiah's dates do not add up
p: The Bible's own numbers for Hezekiah's reign clash. Scholars have tried several ways to fit them together.
b: This verse puts Hezekiah's first year in Hoshea's third year, and 18:9–10 has Samaria fall in his sixth year, about 722 BC. That would make him king by about 727. But 18:13 dates Sennacherib's invasion, firmly fixed by Assyrian records to 701 BC, to his fourteenth year, which would make him king in 715. Both cannot be right as they stand. Edwin Thiele kept 715 and judged the Hoshea links a later miscalculation; others propose a co-regency with his father Ahaz, or keep 727 and suspect that "fourteenth" was worked out from 20:6 (fifteen added years out of twenty-nine). See the topic page on dating the kings.

a: in everything just as his forefather David had done
p: Only a few kings of Judah are praised as doing right "like David." Hezekiah is one of the last two.
b: Kings judges each ruler of Judah against David. Many "did what was right" with a catch ("only, the high places were not removed"; 12:3; 14:4; 15:4; 15:35). Asa was compared with David (1 Kings 15:11), but only Hezekiah and Josiah (22:2) get the comparison with no catch at all. The two of them frame the end of the book: the reformer before Manasseh and the reformer after him. The Hebrew says "David his father"; this translation says "forefather" because David lived about three hundred years earlier.

a: He was the one who took away the high places
t: The first king to close the high places
p: Earlier good kings left the local shrines standing. Hezekiah closed them, and digs at Arad and Beersheba may show it.
b: Again and again Kings says of Judah's good kings, "the high places were not removed" (1 Kings 22:43; 2 Kings 12:3; 15:35). Hezekiah is the first to remove them, and the Rabshakeh will throw it back at him (18:22). Archaeologists have found what may be traces of this. At Arad, a shrine with an altar and standing stones inside a royal fortress was put out of use and covered over in the late 700s. At Beersheba, a large altar with horns was taken apart and its stones reused in a wall. Yohanan Aharoni linked both to Hezekiah. The dates are still argued, and some tie the Arad shrine to Josiah (23:8) instead, but the finds show that shrines like these existed and were shut down.

a: People called it Nehushtan
p: The name plays on two Hebrew words, nechoshet (bronze) and nachash (snake). It may be a scornful nickname.
b: Moses made the bronze snake in the wilderness so that bitten people could look at it and live (Numbers 21:8–9). By Hezekiah's day it had become an object of worship, with incense burned to it. The name Nechushtan sounds like both "bronze" and "snake." The Hebrew says "he called it" or "one called it," so the name may be what worshipers called it, or Hezekiah's put-down: "a mere piece of bronze." The rabbis praised him for smashing it (Bavli Pesachim 56a; Berakhot 10b). Jesus later compares his own lifting up to the snake on the pole (John 3:14).
orig: נְחֻשְׁתָּן (Nechushtan); compare נְחֹשֶׁת (nechoshet, bronze) and נָחָשׁ (nachash, snake)

a: none after him was like him, and none who came before him
t: Two kings who had no equal?
p: Hezekiah is said to have no equal before or after. So is Josiah (23:25). How can both be true?
b: The same kind of praise is given to Josiah: "No king before him was like him ... And none like him rose up after him" (23:25). Readers have handled this in several ways. Many note that each king is unmatched in a different way: Hezekiah in trust (the word opens this verse and runs through chapters 18–19), Josiah in keeping the law of Moses. Others take the phrase as a stock way of giving high praise, as with Solomon's wisdom (1 Kings 3:12). Critical scholars who think Kings was edited in stages often see the two verses as written by different hands, one praising Hezekiah and a later one Josiah.

a: He held on to the LORD
p: The verb is dabaq, "cling, stick to," the word Deuteronomy uses for loyalty to God.
b: Dabaq is the word for a man clinging to his wife (Genesis 2:24) and Ruth clinging to Naomi (Ruth 1:14). Deuteronomy makes it the word for loyalty to God: "hold on to him" (Deuteronomy 10:20; 11:22; 13:4; 30:20). The same verb was used in a bad sense of Solomon, who "held on" to his foreign wives (1 Kings 11:2). So Hezekiah is described in Deuteronomy's language, as the faithful opposite of Solomon.

a: He rebelled against the king of Assyria
p: When Sargon II died in battle in 705 BC, revolts broke out across the Assyrian empire. Hezekiah joined in.
b: Judah had been a paying vassal of Assyria since Ahaz (16:7–8). In 705 BC Sargon II was killed in battle, and his body was not recovered, a terrible omen. Babylon under Merodach-baladan (20:12) and the cities of the west rose up. Sennacherib's own annals say the people of Ekron handed their pro-Assyrian king Padi to Hezekiah, who held him in Jerusalem. Isaiah warned against the alliance with Egypt that came with it (Isaiah 30:1–5; 31:1–3). The narrator calls the revolt a sign that "the LORD was with him"; the prophet Isaiah, in his own book, was more doubtful of the plans that went with it.

a: He struck down the Philistines all the way to Gaza
p: Assyrian records confirm that Hezekiah meddled in the Philistine cities before 701 BC.
b: Padi of Ekron, handed over to Hezekiah by his own people (see the note on 18:7), was freed after the campaign, and Sennacherib and gave towns taken from Judah to the kings of Ashdod, Ekron and Gaza. So this verse fits a real moment, when Hezekiah tried to lead the coast against Assyria. 2 Chronicles 28:18 tells of the Philistines taking Judean towns under Ahaz; Hezekiah may have been winning them back. "From lookout tower to walled town" means every kind of settlement, the smallest to the largest.

a: It was King Hezekiah's fourth year
t: The fall of Samaria, told again
p: The fall of the north is told a second time, now dated by Hezekiah's reign, to set up a contrast.
b: The siege and fall of Samaria were already told in 17:3–6 (see the notes there). The narrator retells them here, dated by Hezekiah's years, for a purpose. Israel fell because "they had not listened" (18:12); Judah, under a king who "trusted in the LORD" (18:5), will be spared when the same Assyrian army reaches its walls. The question the Rabshakeh asks, "Did they rescue Samaria from my hand?" (18:34), depends on this reminder.

a: Sennacherib king of Assyria marched on all the walled towns of Judah
p: Sennacherib's annals tell the same campaign from Assyria's side: 46 towns taken and Hezekiah shut in "like a bird in a cage."
b: The campaign of 701 BC is told in Sennacherib's annals, found on clay prisms (the Taylor Prism, the Oriental Institute Prism and the Jerusalem Prism). In them Sennacherib says he besieged and took 46 of Hezekiah's walled towns and countless villages, using ramps, battering rams and sappers, and carried off 200,150 people with their animals. He says he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem, his royal city, like a bird in a cage, and blocked anyone leaving the gate. He then says Hezekiah sent tribute after him to Nineveh: gold, silver, gems, furniture inlaid with ivory, and his daughters and palace women. The annals never claim to have taken Jerusalem.

a: at Lachish
t: The siege of Lachish in stone
p: Sennacherib decorated a room of his palace with the siege of Lachish. The siege ramp still stands at the site.
b: Lachish, about 30 miles southwest of Jerusalem, was Judah's second city. Sennacherib lined a room in his palace at Nineveh with carved stone panels of its siege, now in the British Museum: battering rams on a ramp, archers, defenders throwing torches, captives impaled, families leaving with carts, and the king on his throne receiving the spoil. A caption says that Sennacherib, king of the world, sat on his throne as the spoil of Lachish passed before him. Excavations led by David Ussishkin found the Assyrian siege ramp of stones and the counter-ramp built inside the wall, along with arrowheads and sling stones, the earliest siege ramp yet found in the ancient Near East.

a: I have done wrong
p: Hezekiah uses chata', the word for sin. Here it means breaking a treaty with an overlord.
b: Chata'ti is the usual Hebrew for "I have sinned." Between kings it means "I have broken our agreement" (compare 2 Kings 18:7 with 1 Samuel 24:11). The Plain's "I have done wrong" keeps the confession. Hezekiah's first answer to the invasion is to admit his rebellion and pay. Isaiah 36 leaves out 18:14–16 entirely, and many scholars think these verses come from a separate, dry record, close in tone to the Assyrian annals. Read in the whole story, they show a king who first tried to buy his way out, and only later turned to the LORD's house (19:1).

a: three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold
p: Kings and the Assyrian annals agree on the gold but not the silver: 300 talents here, 800 in Sennacherib's account.
b: A talent was the largest weight, about 75 pounds (34 kg) on the common standard. Thirty talents of gold is a little over a ton. Sennacherib's annals also give thirty talents of gold but list 800 talents of silver, plus a long list of other goods. Some explain the difference by two weight standards, a heavy and a light talent; others think the annals added in other silver, or simply inflated the figure, as royal inscriptions often did. In Kings the payment comes before the Rabshakeh's speech; in the annals it is sent after the campaign to Nineveh. Either way, the two sources agree that Judah paid and Jerusalem was not taken.

a: the doorposts that he, Hezekiah king of Judah, had overlaid
p: Hezekiah strips the very gold he had put on the temple doors. The rabbis listed this among his failings.
b: The Hebrew simply says the doorposts "which Hezekiah had overlaid"; the metal is not named, but gold is meant, as in 1 Kings 6:32–35. The repeated name, "he, Hezekiah king of Judah," stresses the irony: the king who adorned the temple now pulls the plating off to pay Assyria. Ahaz and Joash had emptied the treasuries before (16:8; 12:18). The Talmud lists six deeds of Hezekiah, three the sages approved and three they did not; cutting off the doors of the temple and sending them to Assyria is among those not approved (Bavli Pesachim 56a).

a: the Tartan, the Rab-saris and the Rabshakeh
p: These are not names but Assyrian titles: the commander-in-chief, the chief official and the chief cupbearer.
b: All three words are Assyrian titles taken into Hebrew. The turtanu was the army's commander-in-chief, second only to the king. The rab sha reshi (Hebrew rab-saris) was the chief of the court officials, often eunuchs. The rab shaqe was literally the "chief cupbearer," by this time a high officer who could lead troops and speak for the king. Isaiah 36:2 names only the Rabshakeh, who does all the talking. His fluent Judean led some rabbis to say he was an Israelite who had gone over to Assyria (Bavli Sanhedrin 60a).

a: with a huge army
p: Since 1886 many scholars have divided chapters 18–19 into three accounts. Others read them as one story.
b: In 1886 Bernhard Stade argued that 18:13–19:37 combines separate reports, and Brevard Childs refined the idea in 1967. On this view, Account A (18:13–16) is a brief record of surrender and tribute that agrees with the Assyrian annals. Account B1 (18:17 to the first half of 19:9, with 19:36–37) has the Rabshakeh's speech and a "report" that sends Sennacherib home. Account B2 (the second half of 19:9 to 19:35) has the letter, Hezekiah's prayer and the angel. Traditional readers, and some recent literary critics, read one story told in stages: payment fails, a first threat, a second threat, and rescue. A harmonizing view (John Bright) kept both accounts as history by placing the angel story in a second campaign around 688 BC, but no Assyrian record supports one, and most scholars now think there was only one campaign.

a: by the water channel of the Upper Pool, on the main road to the Launderers' Field
t: The same spot where Isaiah met Ahaz
p: Isaiah once met King Ahaz at this very channel and urged him to trust God. Now Assyria stands there.
b: Isaiah 7:3 sends the prophet to meet Ahaz "at the end of the channel of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderers' Field." There Isaiah told Ahaz not to fear the kings of Aram and Israel and to trust God, and Ahaz chose instead to call in Assyria (16:7). A generation later, Assyria's spokesman stands on the same spot and asks Ahaz's son what he trusts in. The narrator does not point out the echo, but anyone who knew Isaiah's words would hear it. The launderers washed and bleached cloth with plenty of water, so the field was likely near a spring or pool outside the walls.

a: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the palace
p: Isaiah 22 names both men: Shebna, who was replaced, and Eliakim, who took his post.
b: Isaiah 22:15–25 condemns Shebna, "who is over the house," for cutting himself a grand tomb, and says God will give his robe and keys to Eliakim son of Hilkiah. Here Eliakim holds that office and Shebna is secretary, a step down, which fits Isaiah's words. In the village of Silwan, across the Kidron from the City of David, a tomb facade carries an inscription for a man "who is over the house" whose name ends in "-yahu"; some scholars have suggested it was Shebna's (Shebanyahu), though the name is damaged. "Over the palace" was the top royal office, like a prime minister (compare 1 Kings 4:6).

a: What is this trust of yours that you trust in?
p: The Hebrew root batach, "trust, rely," comes eight times in the Rabshakeh's speech. It is the chapter's real subject.
b: The narrator said Hezekiah "trusted in the LORD" (18:5). Then the Rabshakeh hammers on the same word, batach, eight times in 18:19–30, and the letter uses it again in 19:10. This translation renders it "trust," "rely," "lean on" and "count on," but it is one word throughout. He offers every possible object of trust (words, Egypt, the LORD, horses) and knocks each down. The real question of the chapter is whether Hezekiah's trust in the LORD (18:5) is foolish, as the Rabshakeh says, or wise, as chapter 19 will show.
orig: מָה הַבִּטָּחוֹן הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר בָּטָחְתָּ (mah habbittachon hazzeh asher batachta)

a: this crushed reed you use as a walking stick
p: Egypt as a reed that breaks and cuts the hand is a picture the prophets also used. Isaiah agreed with the Rabshakeh about Egypt.
b: Reeds grew thick along the Nile, so the image fits Egypt well. A reed cane looks like support, but when it splits, the leaning man gets a hand full of splinters. Ezekiel uses the same picture for Egypt in Zedekiah's day (Ezekiel 29:6–7). The Rabshakeh is, in fact, saying what Isaiah said: doom to the ones "going down to Egypt for help" (Isaiah 31:1; compare Isaiah 30:1–7). The enemy is right about Egypt and wrong about the LORD. At this time Egypt was ruled by the Cushite (Nubian) kings of the 25th Dynasty, whose army did march out in 701 (19:9).

a: aren't his high places and altars the very ones Hezekiah has done away with?
p: To many people in Judah, closing the LORD's local altars looked like an insult to the LORD. The Rabshakeh uses that.
b: From the narrator's point of view, removing the high places was Hezekiah's great act of faithfulness (18:4). But the Rabshakeh may have known that many Judeans saw it differently, as many commentators suggest (see the box on the chapter 18 page). The high places had been altars of the LORD in towns all over the land for centuries; Samuel and Solomon used them (1 Samuel 9:12–14; 1 Kings 3:2–4). Closing them and requiring worship at the single altar in Jerusalem could look like robbing the LORD of his honor. So the Assyrian argues that the LORD is angry with Hezekiah, not on his side. Whether or not it was true, it was a shrewd attempt to split the people from their king. The demand for one altar matches Deuteronomy 12:13–14.

a: It was the LORD who said to me
p: The Rabshakeh claims the LORD sent him. Isaiah said something close: Assyria was the rod of God's anger.
b: Assyrian kings often claimed that the gods of a conquered land had abandoned it to them. Here the claim is aimed at Judah's own God. The strange thing is that Isaiah had said nearly the same: "Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger" (Isaiah 10:5), sent against "a godless nation." But Isaiah went on that Assyria did not understand its role and would be punished for its pride (Isaiah 10:7–15). Chapter 19 answers in exactly those terms: the LORD did plan Assyria's conquests long ago (19:25), but the king's arrogance has reached his ears (19:28).

a: in Aramaic
p: By the 700s BC Aramaic was the shared language of trade and government across the Near East. Ordinary Judeans did not speak it.
b: Aramaic, a sister language of Hebrew, spread with the Arameans and was taken up by the Assyrian empire for letters and administration. Officials like Eliakim learned it; the soldiers on the wall did not. "Judean" (yehudit) is the Hebrew spoken in Judah (compare Nehemiah 13:24). Later, after the exile, Aramaic became the everyday language of many Jews, which is why parts of Ezra and Daniel are written in it. The Rabshakeh refuses, because his real audience is the ordinary people.

a: Make a blessing with me
p: Berakhah, "blessing," here means a peace agreement sealed with a gift. In plain terms: surrender.
b: Berakhah can mean a present that seals goodwill (Genesis 33:11; 1 Samuel 25:27). Here it means a peace treaty, and "come out to me" means open the gates and surrender. The offer then borrows Israel's own picture of peace, each man "under his own vine and his own fig tree" (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4). The catch comes at once in 18:32: the good life will last only until the deportation.
orig: עֲשׂוּ־אִתִּי בְרָכָה ('asu itti verakhah), "make a blessing with me"

a: until I come and take you away to a land like your own land
p: Assyria moved whole populations to break national loyalties. The Rabshakeh presents exile as a fair trade.
b: From Tiglath-pileser III onward, Assyria deported conquered peoples and resettled them far away, often swapping populations, as happened with Samaria (17:24). Reliefs, including the Lachish panels, show families walking with their goods and animals, not chained captives. The Rabshakeh even paints the new land in words like Moses' description of the promised land, "a land of olive oil and honey" (Deuteronomy 8:8). What he offers is life, "Live, and don't die!", but life without the land, the temple or the LORD's promise.

a: Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad?
p: Every city named had fallen to Assyria within living memory.
b: Arpad, in northern Syria, fell to Tiglath-pileser III in 740 BC. Hamath on the Orontes was crushed by Sargon II in 720. Sepharvaim and Ivvah appear again in 17:24 and 17:31 as homelands of people resettled in Samaria; their locations are uncertain. Hena is unknown. The Rabshakeh's logic is the logic of the ancient world: a city's god protects it, and when the city falls, its god has failed. Samaria is last on the list. The LORD is treated as one more local god, and that is what Hezekiah's prayer answers (19:15–19).

a: Which one of all the gods of these lands has rescued his land from my hand?
p: Judith gives its Assyrian king and general the Rabshakeh's boasts, and they fail the same way.
b: Judith, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, tells of another Assyrian army sent against Judea, and it echoes this chapter. Its king is "the great king, the lord of the whole earth," and he sends out "men who trust in their own strength" (Judith 2:5). The Rabshakeh, too, spoke for "the great king" and mocked Hezekiah's trust (18:19). The general Holofernes goes further: "Who is god except Nebuchadnezzar?" and "their God will not rescue them" (Judith 6:2). In both books the boast is the enemy's mistake. Here the angel of the LORD strikes the camp (19:35). In Judith, God saves his people by a woman's hand.

a: the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz
p: Isaiah is the only one of the great writing prophets named in Kings. Here the two books share a story.
b: Kings names many prophets, but of those whose books we have, only Jonah (14:25) and Isaiah appear. Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem from about 740 BC, in the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Isaiah 1:1). Chapters 18:13–20:19 appear again, almost word for word, as Isaiah 36–39. Most scholars think the story was written first for Kings and copied into Isaiah, where it closes the first part of the book; some think the reverse. Jewish tradition made Amoz a brother of King Amaziah, so that Isaiah was of royal blood (Bavli Megillah 10b).

a: The children have come right to the mouth of the womb, but there is no strength to push them out
p: A proverb for a crisis at its peak with no strength left. In those days a stuck birth often killed mother and child.
b: Hezekiah compares Jerusalem to a woman in labor who cannot deliver: the moment has come, but there is no strength to finish. Without modern medicine this was deadly. Hosea uses the same image for a people who will not be born (Hosea 13:13), and Isaiah answers it later: "Would I bring a child to the point of birth and not let it be born?" (Isaiah 66:9). The Hebrew mashber, "opening of the womb," can also mean "breakers" of the sea.

a: insult the living God
p: The Hebrew verb charaf, "insult, taunt," is the one David used of Goliath. The story echoes on purpose.
b: When Goliath taunted Israel, David asked, "Who is this uncircumcised Philistine anyway, to insult the battle lines of the living God?" (1 Samuel 17:26; compare 1 Samuel 17:36). Hezekiah uses the same verb, charaf, and the same title, "the living God," here and in 19:16. The Rabshakeh is a new Goliath, a giant of an empire mocking a small people, and the reader is invited to expect the same outcome. "The living God" also sets up the contrast in 19:18 with gods that are only wood and stone.

a: the remnant still here
p: After Sennacherib took Judah's other towns, Jerusalem was what remained. Isaiah built a theme on that word.
b: Sennacherib's annals boast of 46 Judean towns taken. Isaiah 1:7–9 describes the land at this time: "Daughter Zion is left over like a booth among the vines ... Had the LORD of Armies not left a handful of us alive, we would have become like Sodom." The "remnant" (she'erit) is one of Isaiah's great themes; he even named a son Shear-jashub, "a remnant will return" (Isaiah 7:3; 10:20–22). The oracle in 19:30–31 picks up the word: from this remnant, Judah will put down roots again.

a: the errand boys of Assyria's king
p: Isaiah calls the Assyrian officers na'arim, "boys," a deliberate put-down.
b: Hezekiah's men are called "servants" ('avadim, 19:5), but Isaiah calls the Assyrian envoys na'arim, "boys, lads, attendants." The word can mean a young servant or a young soldier, but after the Rabshakeh's swagger it lands as contempt: the empire's great officers are only the king's errand boys. Their words are not truly a threat to God; they are "reviling" him, a word for insult and blasphemy.
orig: נַעֲרֵי מֶלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר (na'arei melekh-Ashshur), "the boys of the king of Assyria"

a: I am about to put a spirit into him
p: Ruach here means an impulse or frame of mind that God sends, as in the story of Micaiah.
b: Hebrew ruach can mean wind, breath or spirit, and also a person's mood or will. God "putting a spirit" into someone means stirring an impulse in him, as the lying spirit in the prophets' mouths drove Ahab to battle (1 Kings 22:22–23), or as God "stirred up the spirit" of kings in other books (1 Chronicles 5:26; Ezra 1:1). The verse tells in brief how the story will end: a report, a retreat and death by the sword at home (19:9, 19:36–37).
orig: נֹתֵן בּוֹ רוּחַ (noten bo ruach), "putting in him a spirit"

a: Tirhakah king of Cush
p: Tirhakah became pharaoh in 690 BC, eleven years after this campaign. The title may simply be the one he later held.
b: Taharqa, a Cushite (Nubian) ruler of Egypt's 25th Dynasty, reigned from 690 to 664 BC. In 701 he was not yet king. Older scholars took this as a slip, and some built on it a theory of a second campaign by Sennacherib about 688 (John Bright). Kenneth Kitchen argued from Taharqa's own Kawa inscriptions that he was a young man of about twenty who came north with the army of his brother Shebitku in this period, so he could have led the force, and the narrator gave him the title he later bore. Sennacherib's annals do report a battle at Eltekeh against the kings of Egypt and the king of Meluhha (Cush).

a: how they put them under the ban to wipe them out
p: The verb is charam, Israel's own word for holy war: devoting a people to total destruction.
b: Hecherim is the verb behind cherem, "the ban," which Deuteronomy and Joshua use for devoting a city to destruction for God (Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 6:21). Moab's King Mesha used the same word on his stele for destroying the Israelite town of Nebo for his god. Here the Assyrian letter turns the word against Israel. The narrator lets the enemy use the language of holy war to show how he sees himself: as the one who decides which peoples live.

a: Gozan, Haran, Rezeph and the people of Eden who were in Telassar
p: These were Aramean cities in northern Mesopotamia and Syria taken by Assyria a century or more earlier.
b: Gozan is Tell Halaf on the Habor River, where Israelites were later settled (17:6). Haran is the city where Abraham's family lived (Genesis 11:31). Rezeph is probably Rusafa, west of the Euphrates. "Eden" is Bit-Adini, an Aramean state on the Euphrates conquered by Shalmaneser III in 856 BC, and Amos 1:5 threatens its ruler. By saying "my fathers wiped out" these places, Sennacherib claims his dynasty's whole history of victory.

a: spread it out before the LORD
p: Hezekiah opens the letter in the temple, as if presenting the evidence to the true King.
b: In the ancient world a vassal might bring an enemy's letter to his overlord and ask for help. Hezekiah does that with the LORD, in the house where the LORD's name lives (1 Kings 8:29). His first response in 18:14 was to send to the king of Assyria; now he goes to the King enthroned on the cherubim. Solomon had asked that prayers made toward this house be heard in times of war (1 Kings 8:44–45). The Hebrew calls the letter sefarim, a plural that can mean a single document.

a: seated on the cherubim
p: The gold cherubim over the ark were pictured as God's throne. Hezekiah prays to the King who sits there.
b: The two cherubim on the ark's lid, and the large cherubim of Solomon's inner room (1 Kings 6:23–28), were seen as the seat of the invisible LORD. The ark is "the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Armies, who sits on the cherubim as his throne" (1 Samuel 4:4; compare Psalm 80:1; 99:1). The Hebrew can mean "enthroned on" or "enthroned above" the cherubim. Against the "great king" of Assyria (18:19), Hezekiah appeals to a greater one.
orig: יֹשֵׁב הַכְּרֻבִים (yoshev hakkeruvim), "sitting on the cherubim"

a: You are God, and you alone, over every kingdom on earth
p: Hezekiah answers the Rabshakeh's claim that the LORD is only a local god like the rest.
b: The Assyrians had put the LORD on a list with the gods of Hamath and Arpad (18:33–35). Hezekiah's prayer denies the list: the LORD is not one god among many but the only God, maker of heaven and earth, and so Lord of Assyria as well. The words echo Deuteronomy's creed, "the LORD is God. Apart from him there is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:35; compare Deuteronomy 4:39). Isaiah 37:16 adds the title "LORD of Armies" at the start of the prayer.

a: only things that human hands had made out of wood and stone
p: Hezekiah uses Deuteronomy's own phrase for idols. Burnt idols prove nothing about the living God.
b: Moses warned that in exile Israel would serve "gods made by human hands, wood and stone" (Deuteronomy 4:28; compare Deuteronomy 28:36, 28:64). Hezekiah turns the Assyrian boast around. Yes, Assyria burned the gods of other nations, but that only shows they were never gods. Assyrian reliefs do show soldiers carrying off the statues of defeated gods. Isaiah mocks the making of such gods at length (Isaiah 44:9–20), and the Psalms say the same (Psalm 115:4–8).

a: Then every kingdom on earth will know
t: Rescue for the sake of God's name
p: Hezekiah asks to be saved not only for Judah's sake but so that the nations will know who God is.
b: This is the aim the Bible often gives for God's acts. The plagues came so that Pharaoh would know the LORD (Exodus 9:16). Solomon prayed that "all the earth's peoples" would know the LORD's name (1 Kings 8:43), and that "every people on earth" would know that the LORD is God (1 Kings 8:60), and David told Goliath that "all the earth" would know there is a God in Israel (1 Samuel 17:46). Hezekiah places Jerusalem's danger inside that larger purpose.

a: the virgin, Daughter Zion
t: Zion as an untouched young woman
p: Jerusalem is pictured as a young unmarried woman whom the conqueror has not been able to take.
b: "Daughter Zion" means Zion herself, the city pictured as a young woman, not a daughter of Zion. Calling her a betulah, a virgin or young unmarried woman, stresses that no conqueror has entered her. She does not cower; she laughs at the retreating Assyrian and shakes her head at his back, a gesture of scorn (Psalm 22:7; Lamentations 2:15). Lamentations uses the same titles for the city after it did fall (Lamentations 2:13). The scorned and the scorner will change places in 25:9.

a: The Holy One of Israel
p: "The Holy One of Israel" is Isaiah's signature title for God, found about 25 times in his book and rarely elsewhere.
b: Isaiah's vision of the LORD on his throne, with seraphs calling "Holy, holy, holy" (Isaiah 6:3), shaped the way he spoke of God. The title "the Holy One of Israel" runs through the whole book of Isaiah, both chapters 1–39 and 40–66, but appears only a handful of times in the rest of the Bible (Psalm 71:22; 78:41; 89:18; Jeremiah 50:29; 51:5). Its appearance here marks the poem as Isaiah's own.

a: the far slopes of Lebanon
p: Assyrian kings really did boast of cutting cedars in the Lebanon and Amanus mountains. Isaiah quotes their style.
b: Royal inscriptions from Tiglath-pileser I to Sennacherib and Esarhaddon proudly record expeditions to cut cedar and other fine timber in the western mountains for palaces and temples. In the Gilgamesh epic, the hero's greatest exploit is a journey to the Cedar Forest. The poem mocks this boasting: the king who claims to master mountains, forests and rivers is a tool in God's hand (19:25). Isaiah 14:8 imagines the trees of Lebanon rejoicing when the tyrant falls.

a: I dried up every channel of the Nile
p: Sennacherib never conquered Egypt. The boast is royal bluster, or looks ahead to his son Esarhaddon.
b: The ye'orim are the branches and canals of the Nile. Sennacherib fought an Egyptian army in Philistia in 701 but never entered Egypt; his son Esarhaddon invaded in 671 BC and took Memphis. The Hebrew name for Egypt here is Matsor, which sounds like the word for "siege," perhaps a deliberate play. The point of the poem is that such boasts are empty: the one who claims to dry up rivers will himself be sent home by the road he came (19:28).

a: I did this long ago
p: The LORD answers the king's boast: what you did, I planned. The verse is a classic text on providence.
b: The LORD tells Sennacherib that his conquests were shaped in ancient days, like a potter forming a pot (yatsar). Isaiah 10:5–15 and 14:24–27 say the same: Assyria is an axe that boasts against the one who swings it. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers have taken such texts as teaching that God rules history even through wicked powers, without excusing their guilt (compare Genesis 50:20). Others find the idea troubling, since it seems to make God responsible for the suffering Assyria caused. The poem itself holds both: God planned it, and the king is still judged for his pride (19:28).

a: I will put my hook in your nose
p: Assyrian art shows conquered kings led by ropes through their lips. God promises the same to Assyria's king.
b: A stele of Esarhaddon, Sennacherib's son, found at Zincirli in Turkey, shows the king holding two small captives on leashes that pass through rings in their lips. Assyrian kings boasted of putting nose ropes on rulers they defeated. Isaiah reverses the image: the LORD will treat the king of Assyria like a captive or a stubborn animal and lead him home. Chronicles says Manasseh was later dragged to Babylon "with hooks" (2 Chronicles 33:11), and Ezekiel uses hooks for Gog (Ezekiel 38:4).

a: And this will be your sign
p: The sign is a three-year return to normal farming. It confirms the rescue after the fact.
b: The invasion wrecked the year's planting. This year the people will live on grain that sprouts by itself from fallen seed, next year on what grows from that, and in the third year they will farm normally again. Some have linked the two fallow years to a sabbatical year (Leviticus 25:4–7, 25:20–22). Like the sign given to Moses (Exodus 3:12), it does not prove the promise in advance but confirms it once it has come true. The farming language then flows into the picture of Judah as a plant putting down roots again (19:30).

a: The zeal of the LORD of Armies will make it happen
p: This exact line ends Isaiah's promise of a child born to sit on David's throne (Isaiah 9:7).
b: Qin'ah is jealous, burning zeal (the Hebrew has no separate word for "burning"), the passion of God for his own. The closing words of Isaiah's great promise of a Davidic king, "The zeal of the LORD of Armies will make it happen" (Isaiah 9:7), appear here too. The rescue of Jerusalem is tied to the promise to David (19:34). For "LORD of Armies" see the note on its first use in this book (3:14). The written Hebrew of Kings has only "the LORD" here; see the variant.

a: for my own sake, and for David my servant's sake
p: God shields the city for David's sake. Some later took this as a promise that Jerusalem could never be taken.
b: The promise looks back to God's covenant with David (2 Samuel 7:16; 1 Kings 11:36) and to Psalms that celebrate Zion as God's unshakable city (Psalm 46; Psalm 48). After 701, when Jerusalem alone survived, many in Judah seem to have taken this as a guarantee. A century later Jeremiah warned against that confidence: "Don't trust lying words: 'The temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD'" (Jeremiah 7:4, compare Micah 3:11–12). The rest of Kings shows the promise did not cancel the covenant's conditions (21:12–15; 25:9). Scholars call this belief the "inviolability of Zion" and debate how early it arose.
r: 2 Samuel 7:16; 1 Kings 11:36; Psalm 46:5; Psalm 48:1–8; Jeremiah 7:4; Jeremiah 26:18–19; 20:6

a: The angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria
p: Readers have explained the angel's blow as a direct miracle, as a plague, or as a theological way of telling a real retreat.
b: Miracle. Jewish and Christian tradition takes the verse at its word: God's angel killed the army, as the "destroyer" struck Egypt (Exodus 12:23) and the angel struck Israel in David's day (2 Samuel 24:16). Judas Maccabeus later prays, "You, Master, sent your angel when Hezekiah was king of Judea, and he did away with a hundred eighty-five thousand from the camp of Sennacherib" (2 Maccabees 15:22), and reminds his troops of the same help in 2 Maccabees 8:19; 2 Maccabees is held as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches, not by Protestants or Jews. Plague. Josephus describes it as a plague (Antiquities 10.21). Just before, he names the Babylonian writer Berossus, but whether the plague detail comes from Berossus is unclear. Herodotus (2.141) tells an Egyptian story that field mice gnawed the Assyrians' bowstrings and shield straps in one night; some think mice point to disease. Theological telling. Many critical scholars note that Sennacherib's annals claim victory and tribute, never conquest of Jerusalem, and never mention a disaster. On this view the story celebrates in sacred terms a real and surprising withdrawal. All agree that Jerusalem was not taken.
r: Exodus 12:23; 2 Samuel 24:16; Isaiah 37:36; Isaiah 31:8; 2 Chronicles 32:21; Sirach 48:21; 2 Maccabees 8:19; 2 Maccabees 15:22

a: one hundred eighty-five thousand
p: 185,000 is far larger than most ancient field armies. Some suggest the word for "thousand" once meant a military unit.
b: No Assyrian record mentions such a loss, which is not surprising, since Assyrian annals never report defeats. Still, 185,000 would be a very large army for one campaign. Those who take the number literally note that it may include camp followers. Others, as with the large numbers in Numbers, suggest that Hebrew 'elef, "thousand," could also mean a clan or a military unit, so the figure might once have meant 185 units, or that the number grew in telling. The Hebrew gives it with no word for "men," just as here.
orig: מֵאָה שְׁמוֹנִים וַחֲמִשָּׁה אָלֶף (me'ah shemonim vachamishah 'alef)

a: stayed in Nineveh
p: Sennacherib lived twenty more years and never returned to Judah. He spent his wars on Babylon.
b: Sennacherib went home and turned to rebuilding Nineveh, his "palace without rival," whose walls held the Lachish reliefs. His later campaigns were against Babylon, which he destroyed in 689 BC. He never came west again. The annals end the Judah campaign with Hezekiah's tribute sent "later" to Nineveh. Whatever happened outside Jerusalem, both sides agree the city did not fall and the Assyrian king did not return.

a: Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, cut him down with the sword
p: Sennacherib was killed by a son in 681 BC. Babylonian and Assyrian records confirm the murder.
b: A Babylonian chronicle says that in 681 BC "his son killed him in a rebellion." Esarhaddon, the younger son whom Sennacherib had chosen as heir, describes in his own inscription how his brothers plotted, fought one another for the throne and fled, and how he won. Simo Parpola identified the murderer as Arda-Mulissi, a name close to "Adrammelech." The text jumps twenty years in one sentence, but the point is plain: the king who mocked the LORD's power to save was cut down in his own god's house, where his god could not save him. "Nisroch" is not known as a god's name; it may be a garbled Nusku or Ninurta. Ararat is Urartu, a kingdom in the mountains of what is now Armenia and eastern Turkey.

a: In those days
p: The illness and the Babylonian visit probably happened before Sennacherib's invasion, though they are told after it.
b: "In those days" is loose. God promises to rescue Hezekiah "and this city" from Assyria (20:6), so the city is still in danger. If Hezekiah reigned twenty-nine years and received fifteen more after the illness, he fell sick in his fourteenth year, the year of the invasion (18:13). But the embassy came because Babylon's king heard of the illness (20:12), so the two dates pull apart. Many historians place the embassy in 703 BC, the few months Merodach-baladan ruled Babylon again; if so, the illness came before the invasion, and the link to the fourteenth year is a schematic count (see the note on 18:1). Others place the embassy in his first reign, 721–710 BC, which would put the illness earlier still. The narrator puts these stories last so that the Hezekiah section ends looking toward Babylon (20:17–18).

a: He turned his face to the wall
p: He turns from everyone in the room to God. The rabbis drew lessons about prayer from this scene.
b: Turning to the wall shuts out the court and the prophet: Hezekiah is alone with God. The Talmud tells that Isaiah announced his death because he had not married or had children; Hezekiah replied that he had a tradition from his ancestor David's house, "Even if a sharp sword rests on a man's neck, he should not hold back from asking for mercy" (Bavli Berakhot 10a). The Targum reads it as the wall of the temple. In the Talmud, one rabbi says he turned to "the walls of his heart"; another, that he recalled the Shunammite woman who built a room on her wall for Elisha (4:10) and was rewarded with a son restored to life (Berakhot 10b).

a: with an undivided heart
p: Levav shalem, "a whole, complete heart," is the loyalty Solomon prayed for and then lacked.
b: Solomon told Israel to keep a "whole" heart with the LORD (1 Kings 8:61), but his own heart was not whole in old age (1 Kings 11:4). Hezekiah claims the quality Solomon lost. Some readers find his prayer self-righteous, a man listing his merits; others hear a faithful servant appealing to the covenant, as Nehemiah does ("Remember me, my God, for good," Nehemiah 13:31). God's reply mentions only his prayer and his tears (20:5).

a: ruler of my people
p: Nagid is the word God used when he first named Saul and David as Israel's leaders.
b: Nagid, "ruler, designated leader," is the title the LORD gives Saul and David (1 Samuel 9:16; 13:14; 2 Samuel 7:8), and the LORD used it of Jeroboam and Baasha (1 Kings 14:7; 16:2). This is its only use for Hezekiah, and it sits beside "the God of your forefather David." The phrase presents Hezekiah as a new David, and the promise to shield the city "for David my servant's sake" (20:6) repeats 19:34. Isaiah 38:5 does not have the title.

a: I will add fifteen years to your days
p: Isaiah announced death; after prayer, God gives fifteen more years. Did God change his mind?
b: The prophet's first word sounded final (20:1). Many Jewish and Christian readers explain that such announcements are conditional, like Jonah's message to Nineveh (Jonah 3:4–10) and God's words in Jeremiah 18:7–10: if people turn, God relents. Others, including some modern theologians, read it as God truly responding and changing course in answer to prayer. Either way, the story makes prayer matter. The fifteen years also bear on dating: twenty-nine years minus fifteen puts the illness in the fourteenth year, the year of 18:13.

a: Take a lump of pressed figs
p: A poultice of pressed figs was a real ancient remedy. The healing uses both God's word and a doctor's cure.
b: Develah is a cake of dried figs pressed together (1 Samuel 25:18). Texts from Ugarit about treating sick horses list pressed figs among the ingredients, and figs were used on sores and boils in later Greek and Roman medicine too. The story does not see a conflict between prayer and medicine: God promises healing, and the prophet orders a poultice. Ben Sira later wrote that the Lord makes remedies come out of the earth, and a wise man will not turn up his nose at them (Sirach 38:4). In Isaiah the figs come at the very end (Isaiah 38:21–22); see the note on 20:8.
orig: דְּבֶלֶת תְּאֵנִים (develet te'enim), "a cake of figs"

a: What sign is there
t: Isaiah tells it in another order
p: In Isaiah the sign is offered before Hezekiah asks, and the figs and his question are tacked on after a psalm.
b: Isaiah 38 has a shorter story: God offers the sign of the shadow without Hezekiah choosing (Isaiah 38:7–8). Then comes a psalm Hezekiah wrote after his recovery (Isaiah 38:9–20), found only in Isaiah. Only after the psalm come the figs and Hezekiah's question, "What is the sign that I will go up to the LORD's house?" (Isaiah 38:21–22), which read like notes added from Kings. In the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), verses 21–22 were squeezed in later by another hand, in the space between lines and in the margin. That suggests the verses were added to Isaiah from Kings.

a: The shadow has moved forward ten steps. Shall it go back ten steps?
p: The Hebrew says the shadow "has gone" ten steps. Many translations read it as a choice: forward or back?
b: The vowels of the Hebrew text make the first verb a past tense, "the shadow has gone (halakh) ten steps," followed by "or will it go back ten steps?" The KJV takes the same word as a question; many modern translations follow a common correction that adds one letter to make it a question (hayelekh): "Shall the shadow go forward ten steps, or go back?", which fits Hezekiah's reply. This translation keeps the Hebrew as it is pointed: the shadow has already moved on as the day goes by; will God turn it back? Hezekiah's answer in either case is that going forward is easy, so the sign must be the reverse.
orig: הָלַךְ הַצֵּל עֶשֶׂר מַעֲלוֹת (halakh hatsel 'eser ma'alot), "the shadow has gone ten steps"

a: on the steps of Ahaz
p: The "steps" may be a stairway whose shadow marked the time, or a sundial. Readers explain the sign in several ways.
b: Ma'alot means steps or degrees. Ahaz may have built a stairway, perhaps to the "upper room of Ahaz" mentioned in 23:12, on which the sun's shadow crept as the day went on; Egyptians used shadow clocks with steps. At Isaiah 38:8 (not here in Kings), the Great Isaiah Scroll reads "the steps of the upper room of Ahaz." As for the sign, traditional readers take it as a true miracle, like the sun standing still for Joshua (Joshua 10:12–14), and 2 Chronicles 32:31 says Babylon's envoys came to ask about "the sign that had happened in the land." Some have proposed a natural cause such as an eclipse or unusual refraction; others read the story as a legend of God's power over time itself.

a: Berodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon
p: Marduk-apla-iddina, a Chaldean chief, twice seized Babylon from Assyria. His embassy was likely about an alliance.
b: Berodach-baladan, as the Hebrew of Kings spells him (Merodach-baladan in Isaiah 39:1), is Marduk-apla-iddina II, a leader of the Chaldean tribes of southern Babylonia. He ruled Babylon from 721 to 710 BC until Sargon drove him out, and again for a few months in 703 until Sennacherib defeated him. Assyrian records call him a persistent rebel. A get-well message from such a man to a western king who was also planning revolt (18:7) was almost certainly about more than health, which is why Hezekiah showed his wealth and his arsenal. See the variant for the spelling, and the note on 20:1 for the date.

a: gave them a tour of his whole treasure house
p: Kings gives no reason for Isaiah's rebuke. Chronicles calls it pride; others see a political mistake.
b: The narrator simply reports the tour and then Isaiah's question. 2 Chronicles 32:25 says Hezekiah's heart grew high after his healing, and 2 Chronicles 32:31 says that when the Babylonian envoys came, God left him alone to try him, to know everything in his heart. Many readers see showing off, the opposite of the trust of chapters 18–19. Others see a political error: by displaying his armory he was joining an anti-Assyrian alliance, the kind of reliance on foreign powers Isaiah always opposed (Isaiah 30:1–2). The rabbis said he ate and drank with the envoys and even showed them the ark (Bavli Sanhedrin 104a).

a: will be hauled away to Babylon
p: Here, in about 703 BC, Isaiah names Babylon as Judah's future captor. That was more than a century early.
b: When Isaiah spoke, Babylon was a junior rebel state under Assyria's heel. Traditional readers see a true prediction: no one in 703 could have guessed that Babylon would later destroy Jerusalem (in 586 BC). Most critical scholars think the oracle, at least in its present form, was written after the fact, by an editor who knew how the story ended, to tie the Hezekiah story to the exile. Some hold a middle view: Isaiah warned that Hezekiah's alliances would end in loss, and the details were sharpened later. Either way, the narrator uses it to point the whole book toward chapter 25, where the treasures do go to Babylon (24:13; 25:13–17).

a: They will serve as eunuchs
p: The word saris can mean a castrated servant or simply a court official. Here it likely means both.
b: A saris was a palace official, and in Assyria and Babylon such officials were often eunuchs. Potiphar is called a saris though he had a wife (Genesis 39:1), so the word can mean just "officer." Here, of captive princes in a foreign palace, the harsher sense is likely. Daniel and his friends were young men "from the royal family" trained under the chief of the sarisim (Daniel 1:3–7), and the Talmud took them as the fulfillment of this verse (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b). Isaiah 56:3–5 later promises eunuchs who keep the covenant "a name that is better than sons and daughters."

a: Is it not good, if there will be peace and safety in my days?
p: Hezekiah's reply sounds to many like relief that the disaster will come later. Others hear submission like Eli's.
b: The most common reading is critical: Hezekiah is glad the punishment will fall on his descendants, not on him, a sad end for the hero of chapters 18–19. Others compare Eli's answer to a harsh word, "He is the LORD. Let him do whatever looks good to him" (1 Samuel 3:18), and hear Hezekiah accepting God's judgment and grateful for the delay, as Josiah's reprieve later is (22:20). Isaiah 39:8 reads "for there will be peace and safety in my days," a statement, not a question. The word emet, "truth, stability," here means security.

a: how he made the pool and the channel and brought the water into the city
p: A 1,750-foot tunnel still carries water from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam. An inscription tells how it was dug.
b: Chronicles says Hezekiah blocked the upper source of the Gihon's water and led it straight down, west of the City of David (2 Chronicles 32:30; compare 2 Chronicles 32:3–4). A winding tunnel about 1,750 feet (533 m) long runs under the City of David from the spring to the Siloam Pool. In 1880 a Hebrew inscription was found near its lower end, now in Istanbul. It tells how two teams of diggers, working toward each other with picks, heard each other's voices through the rock and broke through, "pick against pick," and the water flowed 1,200 cubits to the pool. Most scholars date the tunnel to Hezekiah. Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron, from pottery and their excavations of the spring's older water systems, argued for an earlier king, around 800 BC; others answer with the radiocarbon dates of plant matter in the plaster, which point to about 700 BC, and with 2 Chronicles 32:30. A few (Rogerson and Davies) have argued for a much later date. Isaiah 22:9–11 mentions the waterworks and blames the people for not looking to God, who planned it all.

a: Manasseh was twelve years old
p: Manasseh is named in the records of two Assyrian kings as a loyal vassal who sent supplies and troops.
b: Manasseh's fifty-five years, about 697 to 642 BC (perhaps counting a co-regency with Hezekiah), are the longest reign in Judah. He ruled when Assyria was at its height. An inscription of Esarhaddon lists "Manasseh king of Judah" among twenty-two western kings who had to haul timber and stone to Nineveh for his building works, and Ashurbanipal lists him among the kings who sent troops and gifts for his campaign against Egypt in 667 BC. Kings is interested only in his religion, but the records show a king who kept Judah safe by staying loyal to Assyria.

a: the abhorrent ways of the nations
p: Manasseh's list of sins in 21:2–7 reads like a checklist of Deuteronomy's bans.
b: Deuteronomy 18:9 warns Israel not to learn "the abhorrent things those nations do" and goes on to list them: making a son or daughter pass through the fire, divination, reading signs, omens, sorcery, spells, and asking ghosts of the dead or spirits that know things (Deuteronomy 18:10–11). Manasseh does almost every one (21:6). He also undoes his father's reform point by point (21:3, compare 18:4), and he copies Ahab, the worst king of the north (1 Kings 16:31–33). The narrator presents him as the anti-Hezekiah and the anti-Josiah.

a: He bowed down to all the army of the heavens
p: The "army of the heavens" means the sun, moon and stars. Was this cult forced on Judah by Assyria?
b: Deuteronomy warns against bowing to "the sun or the moon or any of the army of the heavens" (Deuteronomy 17:3; compare Deuteronomy 4:19). Manasseh even builds altars to them in the temple courts (21:5); later Josiah finds horses and chariots of the sun (23:11). An older scholarly view held that Assyria imposed its gods on vassals and that Manasseh's cults were signs of submission. Morton Cogan argued in 1974 that Assyria did not usually require this of vassals like Judah, so Manasseh's cults were his own choice, drawing on Aramean, Assyrian and older local religion. Many scholars now agree.

a: He made his son pass through the fire
p: Like his grandfather Ahaz (16:3), Manasseh gave a son to the fire. Chronicles says sons, in the Valley of Ben-hinnom.
b: 2 Chronicles 33:6 says he made "his sons" pass through the fire in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, the place Josiah later defiles (23:10). Whether "passing through the fire" meant burning a child to death as a sacrifice, or a ceremony of dedication, is debated; most scholars now think Jeremiah's words, "burn their sons and their daughters in the fire" (Jeremiah 7:31), settle that it meant sacrifice. See the topic on Molech. Amon, who succeeded him, was born late in Manasseh's reign (21:19), so the son in this verse was another child, and the verse implies Manasseh lost at least one child this way.

a: ghosts of the dead and spirits that know things
p: Ov and yidde'oni are the spirits of the dead that a medium called up, and by extension the people who did it.
b: An ov is the ghost of a dead person summoned to speak, as at Endor (1 Samuel 28:7–8); a yidde'oni is a "knowing" spirit, one that knows secrets. The same words can mean the mediums who deal with them. The Hebrew says Manasseh "made" an ov, which probably means he appointed such practitioners or set up a pit or shrine for them. Saul banned them and then went to one (1 Samuel 28:3, 28:9); Josiah sweeps them away (23:24).

a: The idol of Asherah that he had carved
p: Manasseh placed an image of the goddess Asherah inside the temple. Inscriptions show some Israelites linked her with the LORD.
b: Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess; the word also names the wooden pole that stood for her (18:4). Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud in Sinai and Khirbet el-Qom near Hebron, from about 800–700 BC, bless people "by the LORD ... and by his asherah," which suggests that some Israelites thought of her as the LORD's consort. To put her image in the house where the LORD set his name was, for the narrator, the deepest offense. It stayed there until Josiah burned it in the Kidron (23:6), and Jeremiah 7:18 and 44:17–19 show women still offering to the "Queen of Heaven."

a: as long as they take care
p: God's promise of the land always came with an "if." Kings uses the condition to explain the exile.
b: The quoted promise sounds like 2 Samuel 7:10, where God promises to plant Israel so they are not shaken again. But Kings keeps adding the condition: "if only" they keep the law (1 Kings 9:4–9). Scholars debate how unconditional God's promise to David was. In Kings, the dynasty's promise seems to stand (25:27–30), but the promise of land and temple depends on obedience, and Manasseh broke it. Judaism and Christianity both later held together God's faithfulness and the people's responsibility.

a: they did worse evil than the nations the LORD wiped out
p: The nations were driven out for their sins. Now Judah does worse, and will suffer the same.
b: God told Abraham his descendants would not receive the land yet, "for the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full" (Genesis 15:16). Leviticus warned that the land would vomit Israel out as it had the nations before them (Leviticus 18:24–28). Here and in 21:11, Kings says Judah under Manasseh outdid the Amorites. The logic of conquest turns against Israel: the same holiness that drove out the Canaanites will now drive out Judah.

a: a disaster that will make both ears ring
p: The same saying announced the fall of Eli's house and, later, Jerusalem's ruin in Jeremiah.
b: God used these words to Samuel about the judgment on Eli's house: "when people hear of it, both their ears will ring" (1 Samuel 3:11). Jeremiah 19:3 repeats them over the Valley of Ben-hinnom, the place of Manasseh's child sacrifice. The echo matters: Eli's house lost the priesthood and Shiloh lost the ark; Jerusalem will lose temple and king. The phrase describes news so shocking that it makes the ears tingle.

a: Samaria's measuring cord and the leveling weight of Ahab's house
t: A builder's tools used for wrecking
p: The line and plummet were used to build straight walls. God will use them to measure Jerusalem for demolition.
b: A qav was a measuring line and a mishqolet a plummet or leveling weight. Normally they are tools for building. Amos saw God standing by a wall with a plumb line, testing Israel (Amos 7:7–9), and Isaiah spoke of justice as a line and righteousness as a plummet (Isaiah 28:17). Here God will test Jerusalem by the same measure used on Samaria and on Ahab's dynasty, which were torn down (10:10–11; 17:5–6). Lamentations 2:8 says the LORD "stretched out a line" over Zion's wall to destroy it.
orig: קַו שֹׁמְרוֹן וְאֶת־מִשְׁקֹלֶת בֵּית אַחְאָב (qav Shomron ve'et-mishqolet beit Ach'av)

a: the way someone wipes out a bowl: he wipes it, then turns it face down
p: A homely kitchen picture: the bowl is wiped empty and set upside down. Nothing is left in it.
b: After a meal, a bowl is wiped out and turned over to dry. The image says the city will be emptied completely and the meal is over. The verb machah, "wipe out," is the same one God used for wiping humankind from the earth in the flood (Genesis 6:7) and for blotting out a name (Deuteronomy 9:14). The kitchen picture and the flood verb together make the threat both plain and terrible.

a: Manasseh shed innocent blood
p: Jewish and Christian tradition says one of Manasseh's victims was the prophet Isaiah, sawn in two.
b: Kings gives no names. The Talmud tells that Manasseh put Isaiah on trial; Isaiah fled and hid inside a cedar, and Manasseh had the tree sawn through (Bavli Yevamot 49b). The Christian Ascension of Isaiah (chapter 5) and the Lives of the Prophets also say Isaiah was sawn in two under Manasseh, and many readers hear this in Hebrews 11:37, "They were sawed in two." Josephus says Manasseh killed righteous men daily and spared not even the prophets (Antiquities 10.38). These traditions are late, but they show how Manasseh was remembered. Jeremiah 2:30 speaks of a sword that "devoured your prophets."
r: 24:4; Hebrews 11:37; Jeremiah 2:30; Jeremiah 26:20–23; Ascension of Isaiah 5:1–14

a: the sin he sinned
p: Kings tells nothing good of Manasseh. Chronicles says he was taken to Babylon, repented and was restored.
b: 2 Chronicles 33:10–17 adds a story Kings does not have. The Assyrian army took Manasseh "with hooks" in bronze fetters to Babylon. "Hard pressed, he pleaded with the LORD his God. Before the God of his ancestors he humbled himself deeply. He prayed to him, and God was entreated by him. He heard his pleading and brought him back to Jerusalem, to his kingship. Then Manasseh came to know that the LORD, he is God" (2 Chronicles 33:12–13). He then removed his idols. Readings: some think Chronicles preserves a real event, perhaps a summons to Babylon during the revolt of 652–648 BC; many think the Chronicler, who links long life to faithfulness, explained the long reign this way. The rabbis argued over whether Manasseh has a share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2). The apocryphal Prayer of Manasseh gives his supposed prayer.

a: the garden of Uzza
p: Manasseh and Amon were not buried in the City of David with earlier kings, but in a garden.
b: From David to Ahaz, the kings of Judah were buried "in the City of David" (for example 16:20). Hezekiah's burial place is not stated in Kings; Chronicles puts it on the ascent to the tombs of David's sons (2 Chronicles 32:33). Manasseh and Amon were buried in "the garden of Uzza" in the palace grounds. Who Uzza was is unknown: perhaps a former owner, or a form of the name Uzziah. Some scholars suggest the old royal tombs were full; others see a quiet mark of dishonor. Chronicles says only "in his house" (2 Chronicles 33:20).

a: Amon's servants plotted against him
p: Amon was killed by his own officials after two years. The reason is not given.
b: Kings gives no motive. Some historians, following Abraham Malamat, link the murder to politics: Assyria's grip was loosening in the 640s BC, and a faction at court may have wanted to break with Assyria, while "the people of the land" wanted stability and the Davidic line. Others suppose a quarrel inside the palace. The narrator is interested in what followed: the rural landowners crushed the plot and placed an eight-year-old boy on the throne.

a: the people of the land
p: In Kings, 'am ha'arets means Judah's landowning citizens, who more than once stepped in to keep David's line on the throne.
b: This group crowned Joash after Athaliah (11:14–20), Azariah after his father was murdered (14:21), Josiah here, and Jehoahaz after Josiah's death (23:30). They seem to be free, landed men of Judah outside the capital, loyal to David's house. Later, in rabbinic Hebrew, 'am ha'arets came to mean an uneducated common person who did not keep the laws of purity, a very different sense. It should not be read into Kings.

a: Josiah was eight years old when he became king
p: A man of God from Judah had named Josiah at Bethel about three centuries earlier.
b: In Jeroboam's day a man of God cried against the altar at Bethel: "Look, a son is going to be born to David's house. His name will be Josiah. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places, who burn their incense on you" (1 Kings 13:2). That word is fulfilled in 23:15–20. Traditional readers see one of the Bible's most striking predictions, like Cyrus named in Isaiah 44:28. Many critical scholars think the name was added to the older story in Josiah's time or later. Josiah came to the throne as a boy, after his father's murder, about 640 BC.

a: swerving neither right nor left
p: The phrase comes from Deuteronomy's law for kings. Josiah is the king who keeps it.
b: Deuteronomy says the king must read the law all his life so that "he will not turn aside from the command, to the right or to the left" (Deuteronomy 17:20; compare Deuteronomy 5:32; 28:14). Joshua is told the same (Joshua 1:7). Only Josiah among the kings is described this way, and the next scene has him hearing a scroll of the law read aloud, as the king's law required (Deuteronomy 17:18–19). For many scholars this is one sign that Kings was shaped by Deuteronomy's ideals.

a: In King Josiah's eighteenth year
p: Kings starts Josiah's reform after the scroll was found in 622 BC. Chronicles starts it six years earlier.
b: Josiah's eighteenth year is 622 BC. In Kings, everything flows from the scroll's discovery: repentance, covenant, cleansing, Passover. 2 Chronicles 34:3–7 says that in his eighth year, when he "was still a young man," he began to seek David's God, and in his twelfth year he began purging Judah and Jerusalem; the scroll is found only later, during temple repairs (2 Chronicles 34:8–14). Many historians think a reform was already under way as Assyria weakened in the 630s and 620s, and that Kings gathered it all around the scroll. Others take Kings' account as simpler and theological, and Chronicles' as reflecting a longer process. Zephaniah, who prophesied in Josiah's days, attacks the same cults (Zephaniah 1:4–6).

a: Shaphan son of Azaliah
p: Shaphan's sons and grandson appear in Jeremiah, and a seal impression of one son has been found in Jerusalem.
b: Shaphan's family served Judah's kings for three generations. His son Ahikam goes to Huldah here (22:12) and later protects Jeremiah from death (Jeremiah 26:24). Another son, Gemariah, had a room in the temple where Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll (Jeremiah 36:10–12). His grandson Gedaliah became governor after the fall of Jerusalem (25:22). In the burned ruins of a house in the City of David, Yigal Shiloh's excavations found a clay seal impression reading "Belonging to Gemaryahu son of Shaphan," very likely the same man.

a: Have him total up the silver
p: The plan for the repairs closely follows Joash's collection box (12:9–15).
b: Under Joash, the priests set up a chest by the altar, and the doorkeepers put in the silver people brought; it was counted and paid to the workers, and no accounts were kept because the men were honest (12:9–15). The same words come back here, including the trust placed in the workmen (22:7). The narrator draws the line: Josiah, like Joash, restores the house of the LORD. The verb here (tamam, "complete") may mean to total the money or, as some suggest, to melt it down into bars.

a: The scroll of the law!
p: Sefer hattorah is a scroll, not a bound book, and torah means instruction as well as law.
b: Books with pages did not exist yet; a sefer was a scroll of leather or papyrus, or any written document. Torah, which this translation renders "law," also means teaching or instruction; it covers stories and sermons as well as rules. The phrase "scroll of the law" is Deuteronomy's own name for itself: "Take this scroll of the law and put it beside the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 31:26; compare Deuteronomy 28:61; 29:21). In 23:2 the same scroll is called "the covenant scroll."

a: I have found it in the LORD's house
p: Most scholars identify the scroll with Deuteronomy. They disagree about when it was written and how it was "found."
b: Which book? Since W. M. L. de Wette (1805), most scholars have identified it with Deuteronomy, or its core in chapters 12–26 and 28. Josiah's acts match its laws: one altar for all sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12), a Passover at the chosen place (16:1–8), the ban on mediums and child sacrifice (18:9–12), and the covenant curses that frighten the king (28). Several church fathers, Jerome among them, had already linked the scroll with Deuteronomy. When was it written? Traditional Jewish and Christian readers hold that it was Moses' law, lost during Manasseh's reign and now recovered. Many critical scholars think it was written in the 7th century BC, perhaps from older northern traditions (Gerhard von Rad, E. W. Nicholson). Some went further and called the "finding" a pious fraud (de Wette, Wellhausen). Others note parallels with Assyrian loyalty oaths of 672 BC (Moshe Weinfeld), while conservative scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen compare its form to older Hittite treaties.
r: Deuteronomy 12:1–14; Deuteronomy 16:1–8; Deuteronomy 18:9–12; Deuteronomy 28:15–68; Deuteronomy 31:24–26; 2 Chronicles 34:14

a: Your servants have emptied out the silver
p: The verb hittikhu means "poured out," probably emptying the collection, though some think it means melting.
b: Hittikhu comes from natakh, to pour. It may mean that the workers emptied the collection chest, or that they melted the silver into ingots for payment, since coins did not yet exist in Judah. Either way, Shaphan's report is all business: the building money has been paid out. Only then, almost in passing, does he mention the scroll (22:10). The quiet way it enters the story makes its effect on the king all the more striking.

a: he tore his clothes
t: One king tears his clothes, another tears the scroll
p: Josiah's grief over the scroll is the opposite of his son Jehoiakim, who cut up Jeremiah's scroll and burned it.
b: Jeremiah 36 tells how Jehoiakim had Jeremiah's scroll read to him; as each few columns were read, he cut them off with a knife and threw them into the fire, "and they did not tear their clothes" (Jeremiah 36:23–24). The contrast with this scene is so close that many think Jeremiah 36 was written with Josiah in mind. Shaphan's son Gemariah even begged Jehoiakim not to burn the scroll (Jeremiah 36:25). Tearing clothes was a sign of grief and repentance, as Hezekiah did (19:1).

a: The LORD's anger is great
p: Josiah hears of the LORD's anger and of curses. Deuteronomy 28–29 fits that description.
b: Josiah assumes at once that judgment is already hanging over Judah because of past disobedience. That fits the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28, which end with exile, and Deuteronomy 29:27: "So the LORD's anger burned against that land, and he brought on it every curse written in this scroll." The Talmud says that Josiah, reading the verse about the king being led away into exile (Deuteronomy 28:36), hid the ark to save it (Bavli Yoma 52b). The phrase "the words of this scroll" comes back again and again in 22:11–23:3.

a: Huldah, a woman prophet
p: The royal officials take the scroll to a woman prophet, though Jeremiah and Zephaniah were active at the time.
b: Huldah is one of a handful of women the Bible calls prophets, with Miriam, Deborah, Isaiah's wife, Noadiah and, in the New Testament, Anna (Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4; Isaiah 8:3; Nehemiah 6:14; Luke 2:36). The king's highest officials go to her without any comment on her being a woman. Why not Jeremiah? The Talmud suggests that Huldah was Jeremiah's relative, and that Josiah hoped a woman would plead for mercy more (Bavli Megillah 14b). Her husband kept the royal or temple robes. The Mishnah names two southern gates of the Second Temple the "Huldah Gates" (Mishnah Middot 1:3).
r: Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4; Isaiah 8:3; Nehemiah 6:14; Luke 2:36; 2 Chronicles 34:22

a: in the second district
p: Jerusalem grew in the 700s BC onto the western hill. Huldah lived in this newer part of the city.
b: Mishneh, "second," names a part of the city (Zephaniah 1:10). Excavations by Nahman Avigad in today's Jewish Quarter found a wall about 23 feet (7 m) thick, the "Broad Wall," built in the late 700s to enclose new neighborhoods on the western hill. Many think refugees from the north after 722, and from Judah's countryside in 701, filled this area, and that it is the "second district." The KJV's "in the college" follows a Jewish tradition (in the Targum) that Huldah lived in a house of study.

a: They sent up smoke to other gods
p: Qitter, "make smoke," covers burning incense and burning the fat of offerings.
b: The verb qitter means to make something go up in smoke: incense, or the fat and meat of a sacrifice. In Kings it is used again and again of worship at the high places and to other gods (12:3; 16:4; 23:5; 23:8). Huldah's charge sums up the whole history: Judah left the LORD, offered to other gods, and worshiped things made by human hands, echoing Deuteronomy's warnings (Deuteronomy 31:29).

a: You will be gathered into your grave in peace
p: Josiah was killed in battle (23:29). How then did he die "in peace"?
b: Some readers see a failed prophecy, and critical scholars often take this as proof that Huldah's words were written down before Josiah's sudden death in 609 BC; no one writing later would have invented a promise of peace for him. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers explain "in peace" by what follows: he would die before the city fell and "not have to see" its ruin, and he was buried in his own grave in Jerusalem (23:30). Others suggest the promise was conditional and Josiah lost it by marching out against Neco, as Chronicles implies (2 Chronicles 35:21–22).

a: the priests and the prophets
t: A public reading of the law
p: Deuteronomy ordered the law read aloud to all Israel. Josiah reads it to the whole people.
b: Moses commanded that the law be read aloud "in front of all Israel, in their hearing" every seven years at the Feast of Booths (Deuteronomy 31:10–13). Joshua read it at Mount Ebal (Joshua 8:34–35), and Ezra will read it again after the exile (Nehemiah 8:1–8). Josiah himself reads, with priests and prophets standing by. 2 Chronicles 34:30 has "the priests and the Levites" in place of "the priests and the prophets"; the prophets here may have included Jeremiah and Zephaniah.

a: beside the pillar
p: The king stands at the royal place by the pillar and binds himself and the people to the covenant.
b: The young king Joash was crowned standing "by the pillar, as kings did" (11:14), so this was the royal station in the temple court. Covenant renewals mark turning points in Israel's story: at Sinai (Exodus 24:3–8), at Shechem under Joshua (Joshua 24:25), under Jehoiada (11:17), and later under Ezra and Nehemiah (Nehemiah 9:38–10:39). The words "commands, decrees and rules" and "with all heart and all being" are Deuteronomy's language (Deuteronomy 6:5; 26:16–17). "Took their stand in the covenant" means the people publicly agreed to it.

a: he hauled their dust to Bethel
p: Josiah carries the ashes of the burned cult objects to Bethel, defiling the old royal shrine of the north.
b: Bethel was the shrine Jeroboam set up as a rival to Jerusalem, with a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28–33). By dumping the ashes of Baal's and Asherah's objects there, Josiah marks it as unclean ground before he destroys it outright (23:15). The Kidron Valley, east of the temple, was a dumping ground for things removed in earlier reforms too (1 Kings 15:13; 2 Chronicles 29:16; 30:14).

a: the idol priests
p: Kemarim is a word for pagan priests, used only for priests of other gods. Zephaniah uses it in Josiah's day.
b: In Aramaic kumra simply means "priest," but in the Hebrew Bible kemarim are always priests of false worship (Hosea 10:5; Zephaniah 1:4). Zephaniah, who prophesied in Josiah's reign, says God will cut off "the name of the idol priests with the priests." These were appointed by the kings, which shows how official such worship had become.

a: to the star signs
p: Mazzalot are the constellations, probably the signs of the zodiac. Mazal tov comes from the same word.
b: Mazzalot appears only here; Job 38:32 has a similar word, mazzarot. It comes from an Akkadian word for the stations of the stars, and in later Hebrew mazzal means a constellation and then "luck," as in the greeting mazal tov, "a good star." Babylonian astrology was spreading in this period, and Isaiah mocks those who "divide up the heavens" and gaze at the stars (Isaiah 47:13).

a: the burial ground of the ordinary people
p: Graves made things unclean. Scattering the dust there made sure the Asherah could never be holy again.
b: Contact with a grave made a person unclean (Numbers 19:16). Throwing the Asherah's dust onto the public cemetery in the Kidron Valley was a way of making it permanently unholy. The prophet Uriah's body was thrown into the same place in Jehoiakim's day (Jeremiah 26:23). The same thinking lies behind filling shrine sites with human bones (23:14) and burning bones on the Bethel altar (23:16).

a: the shrine men
p: Qedeshim were men attached to shrines. Older translations call them male prostitutes, but that is debated.
b: Qadesh means "consecrated one." The KJV calls them "sodomites," and many modern versions "male shrine prostitutes," following the belief that sex rites were part of Canaanite worship. Recent studies (for example Stephanie Budin and Joan Westenholz) argue that there is little hard evidence for sacred prostitution in the ancient Near East, and that qedeshim may simply have been cult staff. Either way, Deuteronomy bans them (Deuteronomy 23:17), and earlier kings had already tried to remove them (1 Kings 15:12; 22:46). The women wove "houses" (battim) for Asherah, probably robes or hangings for her image: the Lucianic Greek is reported to read "robes," which supports reading baddim, "linen garments" (see the variant).

a: From Geba all the way to Beersheba
p: Geba in the north and Beersheba in the south marked Judah's borders, as "Dan to Beersheba" once marked all Israel's.
b: Geba lay a few miles north of Jerusalem in Benjamin, on Judah's northern edge (1 Kings 15:22); Beersheba was the southern frontier. Josiah brought the priests of these local shrines to Jerusalem and made their altars unclean so they could not be used again. This fulfills Deuteronomy's demand to offer sacrifices only at the chosen place: "Be careful not to offer up your burnt offerings in any place you happen to see" (Deuteronomy 12:13). The shrine at Arad, in the south, may have been closed by this reform or by Hezekiah's (see 18:4).

a: the gate shrines
t: Shrines of the gates, or of the goat-demons?
p: The Hebrew says "high places of the gates." Many scholars change one letter to read "of the goat-demons."
b: City gates were public places, and archaeologists have found small shrines at gates, for example at Tel Dan. So "high places of the gates" makes sense. But many scholars suggest reading se'irim, "goat-demons," instead of she'arim, "gates" (the words differ by one small letter and the dot on the first letter), since Leviticus 17:7 and 2 Chronicles 11:15 mention sacrifices to se'irim. No manuscript has it; it is a scholar's guess. Joshua "the city's governor" is otherwise unknown. Seal impressions with the title "governor of the city" have been found in Jerusalem.

a: those priests of the high places never went up to the LORD's altar
p: Deuteronomy lets a Levite from the countryside serve at the central altar. Josiah's high-place priests could not.
b: Deuteronomy says that a Levite who comes from his town to the chosen place "may serve in the name of the LORD his God, like all his fellow Levites who stand there before the LORD" (Deuteronomy 18:7). Here, the priests of the closed shrines are given a share of the priests' food ("bread made without yeast," Leviticus 6:16) but are not allowed to serve at the altar. Wellhausen took this as evidence that the Jerusalem priests resisted Deuteronomy's law. Others think these priests were unfit because they had served at shrines tainted by idolatry, as Ezekiel 44:10–14 later says of Levites who went astray.

a: Topheth, in the Valley of Ben-hinnom
p: The valley where children were burned became, by Jesus' day, the name for hell: Gehenna.
b: Topheth, perhaps meaning "hearth," was the fire place in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, south of Jerusalem, where children were "passed through the fire" (21:6; Jeremiah 7:31). Jeremiah said it would be called the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 7:32; 19:6). Josiah made it unclean, but Jeremiah's words suggest the practice came back after him. The Hebrew name Ge-Hinnom, "Valley of Hinnom," became Greek Gehenna, the place of fiery judgment in Jesus' teaching (Mark 9:43–48). The written Hebrew has "sons of Hinnom," the read text "son of Hinnom"; the meaning is the same.

a: the horses the kings of Judah had set up for the sun
p: Horses and chariots dedicated to the sun stood at the temple entrance. Ezekiel saw men bowing to the sun there too.
b: In many ancient religions the sun god drove a chariot across the sky. Ezekiel saw about twenty-five men in the temple court with their backs to the temple, bowing east to the sun (Ezekiel 8:16). Clay horse figurines, some with a disk on the forehead, have been found in Jerusalem from this period, and some scholars (for example J. Glen Taylor) connect them with this cult, though the link is uncertain. Taylor and others have also argued that some in Judah thought of the LORD himself in sun imagery (compare Psalm 84:11); Josiah's reform rejects that.

a: out in the Parbar
p: Parbar is a rare word, perhaps meaning a colonnade or open court on the temple's west side.
b: The word appears only here (plural) and in 1 Chronicles 26:18, of a place on the west side of the temple. It may be a Persian loanword meaning "open court" or "colonnade," though that would be odd before the Persian period; others connect it with an Egyptian or Akkadian word. Translations guess: "suburbs" (KJV), "precincts" or "court." This translation keeps the name, since no one knows what it was.

a: He rushed them away from there
p: The Hebrew verb looks like "he ran," which is awkward. Many scholars read it as "he crushed them."
