b: The Hebrew vayyarots normally means "and he ran." Taken that way, the king hurried the broken altars off. Many scholars change the vowels and add a suffix to read vayrattsem (וַיְרַצֵּם), "he crushed them," which fits "threw their dust" better (compare 23:6, 23:15). The KJV's "brake them down from thence" reflects that understanding. The Plain keeps the Hebrew verb. The "upper room of Ahaz" may be the room whose steps marked the shadow in Hezekiah's sign (20:11).

a: the Mount of Destruction
t: A pun on the Mount of Olives
p: The Mount of Olives was called the "Mount of Anointing" (mishchah). Here it is the "Mount of Destruction" (mashchit).
b: Solomon built shrines for his wives' gods on "the mountain facing Jerusalem" (1 Kings 11:7), the Mount of Olives. The Mishnah calls it Har ha-Mishchah, "Mount of Anointing" (Mishnah Parah 3:6), from the olive oil produced there. Changing one sound gives Har ha-Mashchit, "Mount of Destruction" or "of the Destroyer," a scornful pun. These shrines had stood for about 300 years, through the reigns of reforming kings like Asa, Jehoshaphat and Hezekiah. "Vile idol" (shiqquts) and "abhorrent thing" (to'evah) are mocking names for the gods themselves.

a: The altar at Bethel as well
p: Josiah's reform reached Bethel and the towns of Samaria, once part of the Assyrian province. How far did he rule?
b: After about 630 BC Assyria's power in the west collapsed, and Josiah seems to have pushed north into the old territory of Israel, which had been an Assyrian province for a century. Bethel lay just across the old border. How far north his control went is debated. Some (for example Nadav Na'aman) think it was limited to Bethel and nearby, while others see a wide expansion toward Galilee; the battle at Megiddo (23:29) suggests he could at least march an army that far. For the narrator, the point is that Jeroboam's sin, which ruined the north (17:21–23), is finally undone by a son of David.

a: just as the LORD's word had said
p: The bones burned on Bethel's altar fulfill the word spoken in Jeroboam's day.
b: The man of God had said of the altar, "They will burn people's bones on you" (1 Kings 13:2). Now it happens. Kings is built around such prophecies and their fulfillments; Gerhard von Rad counted many of them and saw in them the backbone of the history. Traditional readers see God's word proving true across three hundred years. Many critical scholars think 1 Kings 13 was written or shaped with Josiah's reform in view. The Greek translation has a longer text here; see the variant. Burning human bones on an altar made it unclean forever (compare 23:14).

a: the prophet who had come from Samaria
p: The old prophet of 1 Kings 13 lived in Bethel. "Samaria" here means the northern region, named after its later capital.
b: The prophet who had asked to be buried beside the man of God was an old prophet living in Bethel (1 Kings 13:11, 13:31). Calling him "from Samaria" uses the later name of the northern region, after the city Omri built (1 Kings 16:24). His request is honored: the bones of the two men, who had met so strangely, lie together and are spared, just as he had hoped (1 Kings 13:31–32).

a: On the altars he sacrificed every priest of the high places who was there
t: The killing of the northern priests
p: Judah's own priests were brought to Jerusalem; the northern priests were killed on their altars. Readers have struggled with this.
b: The text marks a difference: Judah's shrine priests were retired (23:8–9), but the priests of the high places in the north were slaughtered on their own altars, fulfilling 1 Kings 13:2. Deuteronomy commanded death for anyone who led Israel to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:6–10; 17:2–7), and Elijah killed the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18:40). Some readers note that these northern priests probably served foreign gods brought in after 722 (17:29–33). Others, Jewish and Christian, find the violence troubling and read it as part of a harsh age that later scripture moves beyond. The Hebrew verb is zabach, "sacrifice," a deliberate and grim echo of 1 Kings 13:2.

a: Hold a Passover for the LORD your God
t: A Passover at the chosen place
p: Passover began as a meal in each home. Deuteronomy moved it to the one sanctuary, and Josiah does that.
b: In Exodus the Passover lamb is killed and eaten by each household at home (Exodus 12:3–8, 12:21–23). Deuteronomy commands: "Sacrifice the Passover only at the place the LORD your God will choose to make his name live there" (Deuteronomy 16:6). Josiah's Passover follows Deuteronomy. 2 Chronicles 35:1–19 describes it at length, with thousands of animals given by the king and nobles. Jews still keep Passover, and Christians see in it the background of Jesus' last supper.

a: since the time of the judges who led Israel
p: Chronicles tells of a great Passover under Hezekiah. Kings says nothing like Josiah's had been held since the judges.
b: 2 Chronicles 30 describes a Passover under Hezekiah, held in the second month, to which he even invited the north, and says there had been nothing like it "since the days of Solomon" (2 Chronicles 30:26). Kings does not mention it. Some think the Chronicler created Hezekiah's Passover to make him a second Solomon; others think it happened, and that Kings stresses Josiah's because it followed the scroll exactly. Both books agree that Passover had long been neglected. The last Passover Kings or Joshua describes was at Gilgal (Joshua 5:10–11).

a: the household gods
p: Teraphim were small family images, used for guidance or protection. Josiah sweeps them away too.
b: Rachel stole her father's teraphim (Genesis 31:19), and Michal put one in David's bed (1 Samuel 19:13). They seem to have been family images, perhaps of ancestors, sometimes consulted for guidance (Ezekiel 21:21; Zechariah 10:2). Samuel had called them as wrong as fortune-telling (1 Samuel 15:23). Josiah removes everything the scroll forbade, including private practices in people's homes.

a: with all his heart, with all his being and with all his strength
t: The only one who kept the Shema
p: These are the words of the Shema. Josiah is the only person in the Bible said to have turned to God this way.
b: Moses commanded: "Love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength" (Deuteronomy 6:5). The word for strength, me'od, appears in this sense only there and here. Kings says that Josiah alone fulfilled it. The rabbis kept the comparison: Josiah is the model of a penitent king. For the tension with 18:5, which also calls Hezekiah unmatched, see the note there. The very next verse turns sharply: even this king could not turn back the anger.

a: Still, the LORD did not turn back from his great burning anger
t: Why reform did not save Judah
p: Josiah turned back to God, but God did not turn back from his anger. Scholars and believers explain this differently.
b: The Hebrew plays on shuv, "turn back": Josiah turned back to the LORD (23:25), but the LORD did not turn back from his anger. Kings' answer: Manasseh's sins had sealed the sentence (21:10–15; 24:3–4). Critical view: Frank Moore Cross argued that a first edition of Kings ended in triumph with Josiah's reform, and that an editor in the exile added 23:26–25:30 to explain the disaster that followed. Prophetic view: Jeremiah said Judah's turning was not sincere: Israel's faithless sister Judah "did not turn back to me with all her heart. She did it only with a lie" (Jeremiah 3:10). A midrash says the people of Josiah's day outwardly removed their idols but kept images hidden behind their doors (Lamentations Rabbah 1:53, on Lamentations 1:18; compare Bavli Taanit 22b).

a: marched up toward the king of Assyria
t: Against Assyria, or to help it?
p: The KJV says Neco went "against" Assyria. The Babylonian Chronicle shows he went to help Assyria against Babylon.
b: The Hebrew preposition 'al can mean "against" or "to, toward." The KJV's "against the king of Assyria" seemed natural until the Babylonian Chronicle was published (C. J. Gadd, 1923). It shows that in 610–609 BC Egypt was Assyria's ally, trying to help the last Assyrian king, Ashur-uballit II, retake Harran from the Babylonians. Neco was marching north to the Euphrates to support Assyria. Why Josiah tried to stop him is unknown: perhaps he sided with Babylon, perhaps he wanted to keep control of the coastal road for himself. This translation uses "toward" to keep the Hebrew open.

a: he put him to death at Megiddo
p: Kings gives one short line. Chronicles tells of a warning from God through Neco, a disguise and an arrow.
b: Kings' terse "the moment Neco saw him, he put him to death" could mean death in battle or execution at a meeting. 2 Chronicles 35:20–25 gives a fuller story. Neco sends word: "What do I have to do with you, king of Judah? Not against you, you yourself, today: I come against the house I am at war with. God bade me hurry. Leave God alone, who is with me" (2 Chronicles 35:21). Josiah disguises himself, like Ahab (1 Kings 22:30), is struck by archers in the valley of Megiddo, and dies in Jerusalem. Jeremiah composed laments for him. Herodotus (2.159) mentions that Neco defeated the "Syrians" at "Magdolus." Zechariah 12:11 compares a great mourning to the mourning "in the plain of Megiddo," which the Targum links to Josiah. The book of Revelation's Armageddon is named for Megiddo (Revelation 16:16).

a: They anointed him
p: Jehoahaz was not the oldest son. Anointing is mentioned when a succession needed shoring up.
b: Kings mentions anointing a king only at disputed or unusual moments: Solomon (1 Kings 1:39), Jehu (9:6), Joash (11:12) and now Jehoahaz. Jehoahaz was 23 (23:31) while his brother Eliakim was 25 (23:36), so "the people of the land" passed over the older son, perhaps because Jehoahaz shared his father's anti-Egyptian policy. Jeremiah calls him Shallum and mourns that he will never come back (Jeremiah 22:10–12; compare 1 Chronicles 3:15).

a: at Riblah in the land of Hamath
p: Riblah, on the Orontes River in Syria, was a base for Egyptian and then Babylonian armies.
b: Riblah lay in the Beqaa Valley on the Orontes, on the main road between Egypt and Mesopotamia. Neco made it his headquarters after Josiah's death and summoned the new king there. Twenty-two years later Nebuchadnezzar used it too, and there Zedekiah was blinded and Judah's leaders executed (25:6–7; 25:20–21). On the reading "to stop his rule," see the variant.

a: turned his name into Jehoiakim
t: A new name from an overlord
p: A king who renamed a vassal showed he owned him. Eliakim, "God raises up," becomes Jehoiakim, "the LORD raises up."
b: Pharaoh gave Joseph an Egyptian name (Genesis 41:45), and Babylon renamed Daniel and his friends (Daniel 1:7). Nebuchadnezzar will rename Mattaniah as Zedekiah (24:17). Neco's choice is interesting: he only swaps the divine part of the name, from El ("God") to Yah ("the LORD"). Perhaps the vassal oath was sworn by Judah's own God. Jeremiah condemns Jehoiakim for building himself a palace with unpaid labor while his father Josiah "did justice and righteousness" (Jeremiah 22:13–17).
orig: יְהוֹיָקִים (Yehoyaqim), "the LORD raises up"; אֶלְיָקִים (Elyaqim), "God raises up"

a: he had to put a value on the land
p: Jehoiakim raised the tribute by assessing each landowner, the same "people of the land" who had passed him over.
b: Menahem of Israel had raised Assyria's tribute by a tax on every wealthy man (15:20). Jehoiakim does the same, taxing "the people of the land" by assessment. There may be an edge here: these were the men who had chosen his younger brother over him (23:30). A hundred talents of silver was a heavy burden, and Jeremiah's attacks on Jehoiakim's luxury and injustice fit a king squeezing his people (Jeremiah 22:13–17).

a: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched up
p: After defeating Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC, Nebuchadnezzar took the west. The Babylonian Chronicle tells the story year by year.
b: Nabopolassar's son Nebuchadnezzar (Babylonian Nabu-kudurri-usur, "Nabu, protect my heir") crushed the Egyptian army at Carchemish in 605 BC (Jeremiah 46:2) and became king that year. The Babylonian Chronicle reports that he marched through "Hatti" (Syria and Palestine) in the following years, taking tribute and sacking Ashkelon in 604. Jehoiakim submitted then. In 601 Nebuchadnezzar fought Egypt near its border, and the Chronicle admits both sides lost heavily; he went home to rebuild his chariots. That is likely when Jehoiakim, counting on Egypt, rebelled. Jeremiah and Ezekiel spell the name "Nebuchadrezzar," closer to the Babylonian.

a: Chaldean raiders, Aramean raiders
p: Aram (Syria) is odd in this list of Judah's neighbors. Some scholars suspect "Edom," which differs by one similar letter.
b: The Chaldeans were the ruling people of Babylon in this period. Moab and Ammon were Judah's neighbors east of the Jordan. Aram, to the north, had been an Assyrian province for over a century, so some scholars think the original read "Edom," since the Hebrew letters r and d look almost the same ('rm and 'dm). Edom did take part in Judah's fall (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10–14). No manuscript of Kings is known to read Edom here, so the Plain keeps Aram. The point of the verse is that the LORD, not only Babylon, sent these raiders, as the prophets had said.
orig: גְּדוּדֵי אֲרָם (gedudei Aram), "raiding bands of Aram"

a: It was for Manasseh's sins
p: Kings blames the exile on Manasseh, who died fifty years earlier. Other books see it differently.
b: Kings says three times that Manasseh's sins sealed Judah's fate (21:10–15; 23:26; 24:3). Jeremiah agrees: Judah will become a thing that makes every kingdom on earth shudder, on account of Manasseh son of Hezekiah and what he did in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 15:4). Lamentations voices the people's pain: "Our ancestors sinned, and they are gone; we are the ones who carry their guilt" (Lamentations 5:7). But Ezekiel rejects the proverb that "The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth go numb" (Ezekiel 18:2) and insists each generation answers for itself, and Chronicles blames Zedekiah's generation for mocking the prophets (2 Chronicles 36:12–16). Many readers hold these together: Manasseh set Judah on a course that later generations did not leave.

a: that the LORD would not consent to forgive
p: The verse says the LORD would not forgive Manasseh's bloodshed. Chronicles says Manasseh himself was forgiven.
b: The verb salach, "forgive," is the word of Solomon's prayer, "hear and forgive" (1 Kings 8:30, 8:50). Here it is refused. Many readers distinguish two levels: the sentence on the nation, which stood, and the fate of the individual king, whom Chronicles shows repenting and being heard (2 Chronicles 33:12–13). Innocent blood was believed to defile the land until it was answered (Numbers 35:33; Deuteronomy 21:1–9). Jeremiah 7:6 and 22:3 still warn Jehoiakim's Jerusalem not to shed innocent blood.
r: 1 Kings 8:30; 1 Kings 8:50; Numbers 35:33; Deuteronomy 21:1–9; Jeremiah 22:3; 2 Chronicles 33:12–13

a: Jehoiakim lay down with his ancestors
p: Kings reports a normal death. Jeremiah predicted a donkey's burial, and Chronicles says he was bound for Babylon.
b: "Lay down with his ancestors" normally means a peaceful death. But Jeremiah said of Jehoiakim: "He will be buried the way a donkey is buried, dragged off and thrown out beyond the gates of Jerusalem" (Jeremiah 22:19; compare Jeremiah 36:30). 2 Chronicles 36:6 says Nebuchadnezzar bound him in bronze chains to take him to Babylon, and Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar killed him and threw out his body unburied (Antiquities 10.97). From the Babylonian Chronicle, he seems to have died in December 598 BC, just before the siege. Some think he was murdered by a pro-Babylonian group; others think Jeremiah's word was fulfilled when his grave was later disturbed. The Greek of 2 Chronicles 36:8, and the Lucianic Greek of Kings as reported, add that he was buried in "the garden of Uzza" (Ganoza), like Manasseh and Amon (21:18, 21:26); see the variant. Kings itself simply does not say.

a: Egypt's king never again marched out of his land
p: After Carchemish, Egypt lost Syria and Palestine. The verse explains why Jehoiakim's hope in Egypt failed.
b: The Wadi of Egypt (probably Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai) was the traditional border between Egypt and Canaan (Numbers 34:5; 1 Kings 8:65). The verse is placed here to explain why no help came for Jehoiakim's rebellion. It is a general statement: Egypt did make small moves later, and Pharaoh Hophra's army briefly drew the Babylonians away from Jerusalem in 588 (Jeremiah 37:5–11), but Egypt never again held the land.

a: Jehoiachin was eighteen years old
p: The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 36:9 says he was eight. That seems to be a copying slip.
b: 2 Chronicles 36:9 in the Hebrew gives his age as eight and his reign as three months and ten days. Some Greek copies of Chronicles and 1 Esdras 1:43 have eighteen, as Kings does. Since he had wives (24:15) and, by 592 BC, five sons (see the note on 25:30), eighteen is far more likely. Jehoiachin is also called Jeconiah (1 Chronicles 3:16; Jeremiah 24:1) and Coniah (Jeremiah 22:24). His mother Nehushta is named again in 24:12 and 24:15; the queen mother was an important figure, and Jeremiah addresses "the king and the queen mother" together (Jeremiah 13:18; 22:26).
orig: בֶּן־שְׁמֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה (ben-shemoneh 'esreh shanah), "eighteen years old"

a: the city came under siege
t: The first fall of Jerusalem, dated to the day
p: The Babylonian Chronicle records this siege. It dates the city's capture to March 16, 597 BC.
b: The Babylonian Chronicle for Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year (598/597) says, in summary: in the month of Kislev he mustered his army and marched to Hatti; he camped against the city of Judah; on the second day of the month Adar he took the city and seized its king; he appointed there a king of his own choosing, took heavy tribute and brought it to Babylon. The second of Adar works out to March 16, 597 BC, one of the most exactly dated events in the Hebrew Bible. The "king of his own choosing" is Zedekiah (24:17).

a: In the eighth year of his reign
p: Kings says Nebuchadnezzar's eighth year; the Babylonian Chronicle and Jeremiah 52:28 say his seventh.
b: The difference is probably a matter of counting. Babylon did not count the months before a king's first New Year as year one (his "accession year"). Judah may have counted them, or used a calendar that began in autumn rather than spring. By Babylonian reckoning Jerusalem fell in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year (Adar, late winter); by Judah's reckoning it was his eighth. Jeremiah 52:28, which counts 3,023 exiles in the seventh year, may use Babylonian figures. See the topic on dating the kings.

a: just as the LORD had said
p: The treasures go to Babylon as Isaiah said to Hezekiah (20:17). Yet 25:13–17 still lists temple objects.
b: Isaiah had said that everything in the royal storehouses would be carried to Babylon (20:17). That begins here. Jeremiah faced prophets who promised that the temple objects would soon come back (Jeremiah 27:16–22; 28:3). Many objects remained until 586 (25:13–17). Daniel 5:2–3 tells of Belshazzar drinking from the gold vessels from Jerusalem, and Ezra 1:7–11 says Cyrus returned 5,400 of them. "Cut to pieces" may mean stripping the gold from items too large to carry.

a: ten thousand captives
p: Kings gives 10,000 here and 8,000 in 24:16. Jeremiah 52:28 gives 3,023. The numbers count different things.
b: Ten thousand (24:14) may be a round total, while 24:16 lists 7,000 fighting men and 1,000 craftsmen. Jeremiah 52:28–30 gives exact figures for three deportations: 3,023 in Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year, 832 in his eighteenth and 745 in his twenty-third, 4,600 in all. Jeremiah's figures may count only adult men, or come from a different list. Among this group were the prophet Ezekiel, who dates his book by "the exile of King Jehoiachin" (Ezekiel 1:2), and the ancestors of Mordecai (Esther 2:6). These exiles, the "good figs" of Jeremiah 24, would shape the future of the Jewish people.

a: Mattaniah, his uncle
p: Mattaniah, "gift of the LORD," becomes Zedekiah, "the LORD is righteous." Jeremiah plays on the name.
b: Mattaniah was a son of Josiah and Hamutal (24:18; 23:31), so he was full brother of Jehoahaz and uncle of Jehoiachin. 2 Chronicles 36:10 calls him Jehoiachin's "brother," a word that can mean any male relative. Nebuchadnezzar gave him the name Zedekiah, Tsidqiyyahu, "the LORD is righteous." Jeremiah promised a future king from David's line whose name will be YHWH tsidqenu, "The LORD is our righteousness" (Jeremiah 23:5–6), a name that seems to answer the weak king who bore half of it.

a: Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon
p: Zedekiah broke his oath to Babylon, trusting Egypt. Ezekiel condemns the broken oath; letters from Lachish show the war.
b: Around 589 BC Zedekiah joined a western revolt, encouraged by Egypt's new pharaoh Hophra (Apries; Jeremiah 44:30). Ezekiel says he had sworn loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar by the LORD's name, so breaking it was breaking faith with God (Ezekiel 17:11–21; compare 2 Chronicles 36:13). Jeremiah urged surrender (Jeremiah 27:12–15; 38:17–18). Letters written on pottery, found at Lachish in 1935, come from these last months. One officer writes that he is watching for the fire signals of Lachish, because he cannot see those of Azekah, the very two towns Jeremiah 34:7 names as the last to hold out.
r: Ezekiel 17:11–21; 2 Chronicles 36:13; Jeremiah 27:12–15; Jeremiah 34:6–7; Jeremiah 37:5–10; Jeremiah 44:30

a: on the tenth day of the tenth month
p: Four Jewish fast days still mark the dates in this chapter: the siege, the breach, the burning and Gedaliah's murder.
b: Ezekiel was told to write down this very date, "On this very day the king of Babylon has leaned his weight against Jerusalem" (Ezekiel 24:2). After the exile, people asked whether to keep fasting, and Zechariah spoke of "the fast of the fourth month, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh and the fast of the tenth" (Zechariah 8:19; compare Zechariah 7:3–5). Jewish tradition ties them to this chapter: the Tenth of Tevet (the siege, 25:1), the fast of the fourth month (the breach, 25:3–4, later moved to the Seventeenth of Tammuz), the Ninth of Av (the burning, 25:8–9) and the Fast of Gedaliah (25:25). Zechariah promised they would become days of joy (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18b).

a: hunger gripped the city hard
p: Lamentations remembers the hunger of the siege in terrible detail.
b: A siege of a year and a half emptied the stores. Lamentations describes children fainting in the streets and asking their mothers for bread, and even mothers cooking their own children (Lamentations 2:11–12, 2:20; 4:4–10), the worst of the curses of Deuteronomy 28:53–57. Jeremiah was given a daily loaf "until all the bread in the city was gone" (Jeremiah 37:21). The fall followed the hunger.

a: through the gate between the double walls, by the king's garden
p: The king fled by night through a gate near the Pool of Siloam, heading east toward the Jordan.
b: The king's garden lay at the southeast corner of the city near the Pool of Siloam (Nehemiah 3:15), at the end of Hezekiah's water channel. The "two walls" may be the walls of the City of David and of the western hill meeting there. The fugitives headed down toward the Arabah, the Jordan Valley, perhaps hoping to reach Ammon. Ezekiel acted it out in advance, digging through a wall and carrying baggage out in the dark with his face covered (Ezekiel 12:3–13). Jeremiah 39:4 adds that they "slipped out of the city on the road by the king's garden."

a: Then the king of Babylon put out Zedekiah's eyes
t: Two prophecies that seemed to clash
p: Jeremiah said Zedekiah would see the king of Babylon; Ezekiel said he would not see Babylon. Both came true.
b: Jeremiah told Zedekiah he would "speak with him mouth to mouth, and his eyes will see his eyes" (Jeremiah 32:4; 34:3). Ezekiel said: "I will bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans, but he will not see it, and there he will die" (Ezekiel 12:13). Josephus says Zedekiah thought the two prophets contradicted each other and so believed neither (Antiquities 10.106–107). He saw Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, then was blinded, and never saw Babylon. The last thing he saw was his sons' deaths. Blinding rebels is attested elsewhere in the ancient Near East.
r: Jeremiah 32:4–5; Jeremiah 34:3; Ezekiel 12:13; Ezekiel 17:16; Jeremiah 39:6–7; Jeremiah 52:10–11

a: On the seventh day of the fifth month
p: Kings says the seventh, Jeremiah the tenth. Jewish mourning settled on the ninth of Av, the day both temples fell.
b: Jeremiah 52:12 gives the tenth day of the fifth month (Av). The Talmud reconciles the two: on the seventh the enemy entered the temple, on the ninth toward evening they set it on fire, and it burned through the tenth (Bavli Taanit 29a). The Ninth of Av became the great day of mourning for the destruction of the First Temple and, in AD 70, the Second, which tradition says burned on the same date. Lamentations is read in synagogues on that day. The date in our calendar was about August 586 BC (some reckon 587).

a: Nebuzaradan
p: Nebuzaradan is Babylonian Nabu-zer-iddin. His title literally means "chief of the butchers" or "cooks."
b: A Babylonian list of Nebuchadnezzar's court officials (the so-called Court List, on a clay prism) names a Nabu-zer-iddin with the title "chief cook," very likely this man. The Hebrew title rav tabbachim means "chief of the slaughterers," which can mean either cooks or executioners; Potiphar had the same title in Genesis 37:36. By this time it named the commander of the royal guard. Jeremiah 39:11–14 and 40:1–6 show Nebuzaradan freeing Jeremiah and letting him choose where to go.

a: He set the LORD's house on fire
t: Ashes in the City of David
p: Excavations in Jerusalem have found the burn layer of 586 BC: charred houses, arrowheads and fire-baked seal impressions.
b: Solomon's temple had stood for almost four hundred years. Its site lies under the Temple Mount and cannot be dug, but the city around it can. Excavations in the City of David by Yigal Shiloh uncovered houses destroyed by fire, among them the "Burnt Room" and a building where 51 clay seal impressions (bullae) had been baked hard by the blaze. One bears the name "Gemaryahu son of Shaphan" (see 22:3). In today's Jewish Quarter Nahman Avigad found a tower with ash and arrowheads of the period. Psalm 74, Psalm 79 and Lamentations are laments for this day.
r: 1 Kings 6:1; 1 Kings 9:8; Psalm 74:3–8; Psalm 79:1; Lamentations 2:6–7; Jeremiah 52:13

a: Some of the poor of the land
p: Babylon left the poor to farm. The land was not empty, and archaeology shows towns north of Jerusalem kept going.
b: Older histories spoke of an "empty land" during the exile, a picture Chronicles gives most fully (2 Chronicles 36:20–21) and that Kings also suggests when "all the people" leave for Egypt (25:26). Kings and Jeremiah say the poorest people were left as vinedressers and farmers, and Jeremiah adds that they were given fields and vineyards (Jeremiah 39:10). Excavations show that Jerusalem and the towns of the Judean hills and Negev were badly destroyed, while sites in Benjamin north of Jerusalem, such as Mizpah and Gibeon, continued with little break. Life went on in the land, poorer and smaller.

a: The bronze pillars of the LORD's house
p: The list of looted objects never mentions the ark of the covenant. Its fate is a famous puzzle.
b: Solomon's bronze pillars, Jakin and Boaz (1 Kings 7:15–22), the Sea and the stands are broken up for scrap. Jeremiah had warned that they would go (Jeremiah 27:19–22). The ark is not mentioned here, and after Solomon's time it appears only in 2 Chronicles 35:3 and in Jeremiah's word that it will not be missed. Theories include: the Babylonians took or destroyed it unrecorded; it was lost earlier, perhaps to Shishak (1 Kings 14:26); Josiah hid it beneath the temple (Bavli Yoma 52b; Horayot 12a); or Jeremiah hid it in a cave on Mount Nebo (2 Maccabees 2:4–8). Jeremiah 3:16 says a day will come when no one will miss it.
r: 1 Kings 7:15–22; 1 Kings 7:23–39; Jeremiah 27:19–22; Jeremiah 3:16; 2 Chronicles 35:3; 2 Maccabees 2:4–8

a: Seraiah the head priest
p: Seraiah is executed, but his son was taken to Babylon, and his descendants include Joshua the high priest and Ezra.
b: Seraiah son of Azariah was the grandson of Hilkiah, who found the scroll (1 Chronicles 6:13–15). His son Jehozadak went too, "when the LORD drove Judah and Jerusalem into exile through Nebuchadnezzar" (1 Chronicles 6:15). Jehozadak's son Joshua became the first high priest of the rebuilt temple (Haggai 1:1; Ezra 3:2), and Ezra the scribe traced his line to Seraiah (Ezra 7:1). Zephaniah the deputy priest appears in Jeremiah as a messenger between king and prophet (Jeremiah 21:1; 29:25–29; 37:3).
r: 1 Chronicles 6:13–15; Ezra 7:1; Haggai 1:1; Ezra 3:2; Jeremiah 21:1; Jeremiah 29:25–29

a: And so Judah went into exile, away from its own soil
p: These words echo the end of the northern kingdom (17:23) and fulfill Moses' warnings.
b: "Israel went into exile from its own soil" (17:23) ended the story of the north. Now nearly the same words end the story of Judah. Moses had warned: "The LORD will march you off, with the king you put over yourselves, to a nation unknown to you and your ancestors" (Deuteronomy 28:36; compare Leviticus 26:33). Solomon's prayer had imagined exactly this, captives in an enemy land praying toward the city and the house (1 Kings 8:46–50), and that prayer becomes the only hope the book offers. Jeremiah 52:27 has the same sentence.

a: Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan
p: Babylon put a member of Shaphan's family, friends of Jeremiah, in charge of those left in Judah.
b: Gedaliah's father Ahikam had saved Jeremiah's life (Jeremiah 26:24), and his grandfather Shaphan served Josiah (22:3). Babylon chose a family known to favor submission. Jeremiah 40:7–41:18 tells the story in detail. A clay seal impression from Lachish reads "Belonging to Gedaliah, who is over the house," the title of the royal steward (18:18); some scholars think this was the same man, serving Zedekiah before the fall. Kings does not call him king or governor; it says only that he was put "in charge."

a: Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite
p: A seal found at Mizpah reads "Belonging to Jaazaniah, servant of the king." It may be his.
b: Mizpah is usually identified with Tell en-Nasbeh, about 8 miles north of Jerusalem, which archaeologists found to have survived 586 and served as a center in the following period. In a tomb there in 1932 excavators found an agate seal with a rooster and the words "Belonging to Ya'azanyahu, servant of the king." The name was common, so the identification is uncertain, but the time and place fit. Jeremiah 40:8 lists the same officers.

a: in the seventh month
p: A royal prince killed Babylon's governor. Jews still fast on the Fast of Gedaliah, the day after Rosh Hashanah.
b: Ishmael was of the royal line, a descendant of David through Elishama, and may have seen Gedaliah as a traitor. Jeremiah 40:14 adds that Baalis king of Ammon sent him. A seal impression found at Tell el-Umeiri in Jordan names a servant of "Ba'alyasha'," probably the same Ammonite king. Gedaliah was warned and did not believe it (Jeremiah 40:13–16). The rabbis taught that his death was as great a disaster as the temple's burning, since it ended the last Jewish self-rule in the land, and they fixed a fast for it on the third of Tishri (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18b; compare Zechariah 7:5; 8:19).

a: left for Egypt
p: Judah's last survivors go back to Egypt, where Israel's story began.
b: Moses' last curse was "The LORD will ship you back to Egypt, on the very road I told you that you would never see again" (Deuteronomy 28:68). Jeremiah 42–43 tells how the survivors asked his advice, ignored his warning not to go, and took him with them to Tahpanhes. Jeremiah's last words in his book are spoken in Egypt (Jeremiah 44). Jewish communities did grow there: papyri from Elephantine on the Nile show a Jewish garrison with its own temple of the LORD around 400 BC.

a: Evil-merodach
p: Nebuchadnezzar's son Amel-Marduk ruled Babylon from 562 to 560 BC. He freed Jehoiachin in his first year.
b: Nebuchadnezzar died in 562 BC after reigning 43 years. His son Amel-Marduk, "man of Marduk," ruled only two years before he was murdered and replaced by his brother-in-law Neriglissar. In Hebrew the name became Ewil-merodach, and ewil means "fool," perhaps a joke. The later Babylonian priest Berossus, quoted by Josephus, called him lawless and wild (Against Apion 1.146–147). Releasing prisoners was a known way for a new king to mark his accession. Jehoiachin's release came in March 561 BC, after thirty-seven years in custody.

a: he lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah
t: A Joseph story at the end
p: "Lifting up the head" means freeing and honoring someone. The phrase recalls Joseph's prison in Egypt.
b: The idiom is rare. Its best-known use is in Joseph's prison: Pharaoh "lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer" (Genesis 40:20) and restored him. Several scholars have noticed that the end of Kings echoes the Joseph story: an Israelite in a foreign prison, raised up by a foreign king, given new clothes and a place at court. Israel's story in Egypt began with a prisoner lifted up; its story in Babylon ends the same way. The echo may be a quiet sign of hope that God has not finished.

a: set his throne above the thrones of the kings
p: The "throne" given Jehoiachin recalls God's promise of an everlasting throne for David's line (2 Samuel 7:16).
b: The word for his seat of honor is kisse', the same word as the "throne" of 2 Samuel 7:16: "Your throne will stand firm for all time." Some readers hear in the word a hint that the promise is still alive. Others point out that it is only a chair at a foreign court, among other captive kings, and that the promise seems further away than ever. Jeremiah had said no descendant of Jehoiachin would sit on David's throne (Jeremiah 22:30), yet his grandson Zerubbabel led the return (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 2:23), and Matthew includes Jeconiah in Jesus' family line (Matthew 1:11–12).

a: he ate bread in the king's presence always
p: Like Mephibosheth at David's table, the last Davidic king now eats at a foreign king's table.
b: David honored Saul's grandson Mephibosheth by giving him a place at his table: "he ate at the king's table every day" (2 Samuel 9:13). Jan Jaynes Granowski (1992) and others have read the end of Kings against that scene, with David's heir now eating as a dependant at a Babylonian table; see the chapter 25 page. Eating "before" a king was a mark of honor and of dependence. Whether that is a sad end or a gracious one is part of the debate over the book's last words (see the note on 25:30).

a: His food allowance was a steady one
p: Clay tablets from Babylon list oil rations for "Ya'ukin, king of the land of Yahudu" and his sons.
b: In 1939 Ernst Weidner published tablets found in a storeroom near the Ishtar Gate of Babylon, listing rations of oil and barley for many foreigners at the royal court. Several name "Ya'u-kinu, king of the land of Yahudu," his five sons, and other Judeans; one tablet is dated to Nebuchadnezzar's thirteenth year, 592 BC. So even before his release Jehoiachin was a kept hostage, and Babylon still called him king. Judeans in Babylonia also dated events by his exile (Ezekiel 1:2), and tablets from a village called Al-Yahudu ("Judah-town"), from 572 BC on, show Judean families farming and trading there.

a: for as long as he lived
p: Kings ends with a captive king fed for life. Scholars still argue whether this ending looks forward or only closes the book.
b: An ending without hope. Martin Noth thought the Deuteronomistic History simply explains the catastrophe as deserved; the last verses report a fact and promise nothing. A small door left open. Gerhard von Rad saw in Jehoiachin's release a hint that the promise to David (2 Samuel 7) was not dead. Hans Walter Wolff argued the book calls the exiles to repent, in line with Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8:46–53) and Deuteronomy 30:1–5. A guide for life in exile. Others read it as a model: serve the foreign king, live, and wait, as Jeremiah advised (Jeremiah 29:4–7). Rabbinic midrash remembered Jehoiachin as a king who repented in prison. Christians see the line continuing to the Messiah (Matthew 1:12–16). Jeremiah 52:34 adds "until the day of his death."
r: 2 Samuel 7:12–16; 1 Kings 8:46–53; Deuteronomy 30:1–5; Jeremiah 29:4–7; Jeremiah 52:34; Matthew 1:12–16
